EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Thu, 26 Nov 2026 07:49:21 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.5 [Interview] Europe’s next budget risks ‘making the strong stronger’ by diverting funds from poorer areas, EU regions chief warns https://euobserver.com/250658/interview-europes-next-budget-risks-making-the-strong-stronger-by-diverting-funds-from-poorer-areas-eu-regions-chief-warns/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 06:38:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=250658 As 2026 draws to a close, EU institutions and capitals are finalising the bloc's 2028 to 2034 budget, with catch-up funding for poor regions likely to face deep cuts, even is its top advocate in Brussels is fighting back. ]]> As the first Hungarian citizen to head an EU institution, Kata Tüttő was predisposed to sympathise with marginalised communities. A former deputy mayor of Budapest, the socialist politician and economist has been heading the European Committee of the Regions since 2025, and now faces the biggest task so far in her role.

Ahead of a crunch summit at which EU leaders will discuss cuts to the EU budget on Thursday and Friday (26 and 27 November), Tüttő spoke to EUobserver about the difficulty of getting Brussels to prioritise investment in Europe’s underdeveloped communities.

What are the risks to the regions under the existing proposals for the 2028-2034 EU budget?

In the cities and regions, the expectations are big, because we have a lot of challenges. There was a feeling in the air that if we have new strategies, if we have new ambitions to become climate neutral, to become strategically independent, to invest in housing. There was a sense that money will follow.

One of the most important policies in the European Union is called cohesion policy. Historically, one-third of the budget has gone into food security and common agricultural policy. Now it’s seen as being really justified that we invested, so European farmers don’t stop producing food. The other one-third is the so-called cohesion policy. It’s the most important investment policy of the EU.

Read more

Shake-up of EU Commission regions department sparks fears for future of cohesion policy

So how it works that we have the single market, we make business together in the EU because there’s a free flow of people, capital, services, goods, but the money is not evenly distributed. So the strong are getting stronger, the weak weaker. When the agreement on the single market was born, it was clear that you need a reinvestment policy which somehow connects all of the part of the European territories to the single market. This is cohesion policy. 

It invests in connecting the territories, connecting the people there, investing in skills, and connecting the businesses to the market. The big change in the architecture of the next budget is that cohesion policy is no longer seen as a standalone European policy, but it is detached from the competitiveness narrative, and is denominated as a national policy.

]]> With no summit deal expected, it is clear the EU budget falls short on ambition – but does it matter? https://euobserver.com/251633/with-no-summit-deal-expected-it-is-clear-the-eu-budget-falls-short-on-ambition-but-does-it-matter/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251633 After months of haggling and negotiation the next seven year EU budget looks devoid of ambition and purpose.]]> Of all the EU’s policy battles, nothing causes more ink to be spilled, is given more reverence and yet is unimportant as the EU budget. There – I’ve said it. 

The income guarantees in the EU budget offer vital financial life-support to millions of European farmers but this week’s budget summit in Brussels, which follows months of painstaking negotiations, will see EU leaders spend two days haggling over the difference of about €30-40bn.  And few expect any white smoke to emerge. 

Read more

Less EU money for farmers and regions, but a growing Ukraine bill: Leaders meet to square trillion-euro circles at special summit

EU budget negotiations have followed a similar pattern for a generation; the EU commission proposes plans to significantly increase spending; the European Parliament demands more still and member states radically pare down the spending plan. The end result is typically a small increase, close to the rate of inflation, with which nobody is happy. 

That pattern – or exercise in futility – is set to play out again this week.

]]> [Exclusive] Details leaked of EU plan to cancel Russian sports in Europe, including Trump Jr.’s boxing pal https://euobserver.com/251647/exclusive-details-leaked-of-eu-plan-to-cancel-russian-sports-in-europe-including-trump-jr-s-boxing-pal/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 17:11:25 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251647 "Russia increasingly uses the fields of sports and culture as ... avenues for propaganda to legitimise its military aggression," said the draft EU sanctions text.]]> Russia is being fully cancelled from European sports, in a cultural counter-offensive that also strikes at the US president’s family, and comes with added financial stings in the tail for Moscow.

“Russia increasingly uses the fields of sports and culture as … avenues for propaganda to legitimise its military aggression, exert influence within the Union and undermine European Union democratic values,” said the EU’s draft 22nd sanctions on Russia, an internal document seen by EUobserver on Wednesday (25 November).

“In addition, Russia’s war of aggression continues to irreversibly damage the cultural heritage of Ukraine,” added the text.

It banned “athletes or sports professionals who compete on behalf of … the Russian Federation to participate at sporting events or competitions on the territory of the Union”.

Russian fans in EU stadiums would still be free to wave their flags and sing national songs to cheer on Russian athletes, who could compete “under a neutral status”.

But it will be forbidden for “organisers, promoters, or athletes and sports professionals to display or present official symbols of the Russian Federation, including flags, emblems, colours, anthems,” said the draft text.

Russian government officials will not be allowed into venues in their formal capacities.

Read more

Nathan Cofnas is just the latest far-right ‘snowflake’ to pretend he’s being martyred in Europe

“It shall be prohibited to allow Russian nationals to hold any posts in the governing bodies of international or … national sports governing bodies established in a member state”, the EU also said.

And there will be “restrictions on acceptance of financing or other benefits from the Russian State or its proxies by Union sporting and cultural associations or entities,” it added.

Switzerland is home to some 70 international sports federations and normally aligns itself with EU sanctions, but the Swiss foreign ministry did not reply in time when asked if Bern would mirror the sports ban.

The International Olympic Committee, in Lausanne, Switzerland, which voted in July to let Russian athletes back into world sports, also did not reply.

But, for its part, the EU will strike a related PR blow against Donald Trump Jr. (the thin-skinned US president’s son), by singling out a Russian billionaire who bankrolled Trump Jr.’s Caribbean wedding in May and went with him to shoot endangered sheep in Mongolia in August – Umar Kremlev.

Kremlev, who heads the International Boxing Association (IBA) in Lausanne, and who made his fortune in car dealing and state lotteries in Russia, will go under an EU visa-ban and asset-freeze, as the only internationally known figure out of the 80 new individuals and 81 entities being blacklisted.

The EU mentioned the fact Russian president Vladimir Putin personally gave him the Order of Friendship medal this year as one reason to scalp Kremlev, while adding that he was “supporting and implementing actions and
policies which undermine or threaten the territorial integrity,
sovereignty and independence of Ukraine.”

The others were mostly minor names in Russia’s defence and oil industries, except for Alexander Stuglev, the head of Roscongress, which runs the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum, an annual Russian business beauty parade, aimed at wooing Western investors.

Kremlev’s IBA did not reply to EUobserver when asked if he would step down after being blacklisted, but Russia’s former head of the International Chess Federation in Switzerland, Arkady Dvorkovich, did give up his post after being listed by the EU in the 21st round in July.

Read more

Weird guests and Ukraine drones make ‘Putin’s Davos’ a PR disaster, despite return of US businessmen

The final sanctions might still change and Slovakia’s pro-Russian prime minister, Robert Fico, as well as Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, have, in the past, vetoed EU culture sanctions, for instance against Russian Orthodox Church patriarch Kirill.

But they will both feel under pressure in Brussels on Thursday to agree the Russia measures, when they come to an EU budget summit, in which Germany, for one, has threatened to withhold “cohesion funding”, which poor Bulgarian and Slovak regions need, unless they get behind Ukraine.

The 22nd round also comes amid blossoming US-brokered peace talks between Russia and Ukraine, in which Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani said on 16 November that the EU could use sanctions relief as leverage to force Moscow to listen to its views.

The draft 22nd round of Russia sanctions contains nothing on wealthy Russian tourists, who still flock to France, Italy, and Spain in growing numbers.

]]> MEPs want billions more to tackle migration in next seven-year EU budget https://euobserver.com/251594/meps-want-billions-more-to-tackle-migration-in-next-seven-year-eu-budget/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:22:30 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251594 MEPs have demanded more than €3bn in additional funding for three key migration and home affairs programmes in the EU's next seven year budget.]]> As negotiators clash over the future of the EU’s €1.8 trillion budget, MEPs are demanding more cash for migration, integration and the shoring up of external borders.

MEPs spearheading three home affairs files and their respective budgets on Wednesday (25 November) presented their arguments for the EU’s next seven year budget for 2028 to 2034.

Their files cover integration, borders and internal security.

The commission earmarked a total of €34.2bn for all three, a ring-fenced minimum. MEPs are demanding an 11 percent increase.

Read more

Less EU money for farmers and regions, but a growing Ukraine bill: Leaders meet to square trillion-euro circles at special summit

Karlo Ressler, a centre-right MEP from Croatia with the European People’s Party (EPP) told reporters in Strasbourg that funding “border infrastructure” was vital.

Ressler, along with Portuguese socialist Ana Catarina Mendes and Belgium’s Assita Kanko of the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR), were presenting their arguments ahead of negotiations with EU governments.

Ressler wants €17.12bn for borders, up from the commission’s proposed €15.3bn.

The money, he said, is needed to fund the development, construction, adaptation, maintenance and modernisation of infrastructure and facilities.

Although the terminology is vague, it doesn’t explicitly cite border walls and fences. Funding walls is controversial given the historical precedents Europe faced in Germany in the aftermath of the Second World War.

Instead, he specifies the need for equipment at border crossing points and along external borders, including fixed, mobile and deployable assets required for border checks, and surveillance operations.

Ressler also highlighted the need for funding to support migration projects abroad to create “stronger operational cooperation beyond the EU’s territory.”

Far right unhappy

The far-right Patriots for Europe Group were not happy.

Fabrice Leggeri, a French far-right MEP who once led the EU’s border force Frontex, faulted Ressler for explicitly including search and rescue but not border fences.

Portugal’s Ana Catarina Mendes focused on integration (as well as asylum and migration) and is hoping to increase the budget to €13.31bn from the commission’s €12bn.

Mendes says at least 15 percent of that sum should go towards legal migration, integration and social inclusion.

“Integration can’t simply be seen as an expense; it’s an investment in social cohesion, the economy, and the future of our societies,” she said.

Meanwhile, Belgium’s conservative Assita Kanko dealt with internal security.

She wants its budget to increase to €7.61bn, up from the commission’s €6.84bn.

Kanko highlighted the need to finance projects to counter instrumentalisation, a catch-all phrase used to describe the ways that hostile states use migrants to destabilise Europe.

Read more

Europe’s rights court clears way to return more asylum seekers to Belarus, after pressure from nine governments

“At the same time, this proposal aims to grant member states more flexibility,” she said.

“The new fund will run until 2034, after all, and a period during which the security landscape could well undergo significant change,” she said, highlighting hybrid threats.

Numbers aside, the boost in budget lines proposed by the commission points to clear political priorities when it comes to reducing irregular migration.

The commission has set out plans to triple its migration budget to €81bn between 2028 and 34. And the three files covered by the MEPs have also increased dramatically.

When compared to the current seven year budget, the figures dealing with integration got a 64 percent boost, the budget dealing with borders a 247 percent boost, while internal security saw its offering climb by 399 percent.

An internal negotiating spreadsheet highlighting the differences, seen by EUobserver, shows that those figures have so far not been disputed or challenged by the Irish EU presidency.

]]> Slovakia’s Fico snubbed Poland and Europe, insulted Ukraine veterans (again), and callously lied about Putin’s war (Ukraine Battlefield update, day 1,734) https://euobserver.com/251560/slovakias-fico-snubbed-poland-and-europe-insulted-ukraine-again-and-callously-lied-about-putins-war-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1734/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:03:32 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251560 As Slovak PM Robert Fico shrugs off war in Lviv and snubs both Warsaw and Brussels, thousands of grieving families, maimed soldiers and fresh Russian strikes in western Ukraine expose just how far his rhetoric has drifted from the front’s brutal reality.]]>
  • An attempt to explain to Slovakia’s prime minister that there is a war in Lviv.
  • The situation in Kupiansk is worsening.
  • New details about the disastrous Ukrainian attack on Toretsk last spring, and a comparison with the current situation.
  • Maps of the day – Kupiansk and Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi; Toretsk in May 2025; Toretsk and Kostiantynivka in November 2026.
  • Videos of the day – Ukrainians received their first Lynx fighting vehicles and shared interesting details about them; the Russians captured Popasna on 7 May 2022, and today it is 40 km from the front line and a ghost town; a pickup truck is missing a wheel, so soldiers replaced it with a tree stump.

    • An attempt to explain to Slovakia’s prime minister that there is a war in Lviv. “There is simply not even a hint of any war in Lviv. The war there is concentrated primarily on the front line,” Robert Fico said on Wednesday (25 November) morning at the Slovak parliament’s European affairs committee, following his recent visit to Lviv, in Western Ukraine.

    He also reiterated to MPs that Slovakia would not support the €45bn loan for Ukraine. He described the European Commission’s effort to split it into two parts, with €25bn going to military aid and €20bn to civilian aid, as “a trick by the Commission”.

    Fico made these remarks just two days after Polish prime minister Donald Tusk called on him to show solidarity with Poland, whose territory was hit by Russian cruise missiles. “I do not know whether this appeal will touch your soul, but I am certain that this issue will determine Europe’s future,” Tusk said about aid to Ukraine.

    This is not the first time the Slovak prime minister has cast doubt on Ukraine’s suffering. While he himself has not yet dared to travel to Kyiv, on 23 January 2024 he nonetheless arrogantly declared: “Do you seriously think there is a war in Kyiv? Surely you cannot be serious. Life there is completely normal.” By then, the Ukrainian capital had already been targeted by air raids for two years.

    It cannot be assumed that Fico lacks the means to verify the real situation in Lviv, so the most likely explanation is that he is knowingly lying. Another possibility is that, under the influence of Russian propaganda, he has completely lost touch with reality. The following lines are an attempt to explain to the Slovak prime minister what city and what country he repeatedly insults with his remarks.

    ]]>         EU commission proposes €50bn tech fund to buy into AI, quantum and other strategic companies https://euobserver.com/251514/eu-commission-proposes-e50bn-tech-fund-to-buy-into-ai-quantum-and-other-strategic-companies/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 14:15:02 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251514 The EU Commission has presented plans to launch a €50bn tech sovereignty fund to take stakes in strategic companies to prevent them leaving to the US or China. ]]> The European Commission on Wednesday (25 November) revealed the first details of a future fund with a target size of €50bn designed to take direct stakes in strategic companies so that they remain in Europe.

    “We are now creating the legal basis so that we can set up such a fund,” said Henna Virkkunen, the EU’s tech sovereignty chief.

    She called the fund’s size a “target” and a “sufficient starting point” which is meant to “leverage” further investments worth €400-500bn, she said. 

    Some member states already have smaller sovereign funds of their own. 

    But investment needs in critical technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum computing or other ‘deep tech’ sectors, “often need investments of hundreds of millions of euros,” she said.

    “We have to really pool our resources in Europe,” she said, adding that the EU does not have that kind of equity fund at European level.

The Brussels executive is expected to propose a cage phase-out plan in December.]]> By delaying its response to requests for a ban on cages for farmed animals, the EU Commission failed to meet its legal obligations, the EU court has found.

    In the first ruling of its kind, the European Court of Justice decided on Wednesday (25 November) that insufficient action was taken after 1.4 million people signed a European Citizens’ Initiative petition to ban cages for farmed animals.

    In its judgment, the General Court in Luxembourg upheld the action of a citizens’ committee seeking a declaration that the commission failed to act.

    The commission is legally obliged to respond to petitions once they reach 1m or more signatures. In 2021, it responded positively to ‘End the Cage Age’ after MEPs also voted to endorse the initiative.

    But the Brussels executive is yet to propose the animal rights legislation that the petition requested.

    Read more

    Poll shows public revulsion on caged hens ahead of EU-ban deadline

    ‘Historic victory for animals’

    The court decision was “a historic victory for animals and for democracy in Europe”, said Annamaria Pisapia, a spokesperson for the petitioners.

    ]]>         A Russian plan to federalise Moldova could give it a window to control access to EU membership https://euobserver.com/251069/a-russian-plan-to-federalise-moldova-could-give-it-a-window-to-control-access-to-eu-membership/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 12:45:15 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=251069 A reported Russian plan to federalise Moldova would hand the Kremlin a lever over who joins the EU. Europe should rule it out before it reaches the table.]]> Moscow’s strategy in its negotiations with Ukraine is no secret. The war’s resolution is no longer the sole subject of bilateral talks, but rather one item in a long list of maximalist demands. Russia now demands a new “security architecture” for all of Europe, with the war’s end a secondary priority. 

    It is not hard to compare this stance with Russia’s December 2021 ultimatum, demanding that Nato members commit to no further enlargement of the alliance and a ban on Nato activity in Eastern Europe. Moldova, yet again, finds itself directly at the centre of Russia’s confrontation with the West. 

    In late November 2003, Vladimir Putin was preparing to fly to Chișinău to witness the signing of the Kozak Memorandum, a Russian plan to turn Moldova into an asymmetric federation in which the breakaway region of Transnistria would hold a blocking vote over national decisions. The plan collapsed the night before.

    Under heavy Western pressure, Moldova’s leadership withdrew its consent, and Putin never boarded the plane.

    Twenty-three years later, the same idea appears to be back. This time, the idea is subsumed within the negotiations over Ukraine. Europe risks watching from the corridor.

    Read more

    War of propaganda: Russia calls Ukraine a ‘burden’ and uses Moldova as a ‘testing ground’ to sabotage EU enlargement

    Russian outlet Eho, citing sources close to the talks, reported this week that Moscow is seeking to restructure Moldova as a federation of Moldova, Transnistria and Gagauzia, with independence referendums in the two regions should Moldova join the European Union.

    The proposal would reportedly also include the withdrawal of Russian troops from Transnistria in exchange for a Moldovan commitment not to join any military alliance. The report is unconfirmed. But its logic fits Russian policy so closely that European capitals cannot afford to dismiss it.

    Read more

    [Interview] Moldova races for EU membership by 2030: ‘We owe this chance to Ukrainians’, minister says

    A veto over enlargement

    The most dangerous element is the referendum clause, because it targets the EU itself. Moldova’s 1994 law on Gagauzia already grants the region a right to external self-determination, if Moldova’s status as an independent state changes.

    The reported proposal would attach an explicit secession trigger to EU membership.

    If incorporated into a settlement, this provision would attach the threat of territorial fragmentation to Moldova’s European integration. The referendum need never take place for that threat to shape accession.

    Any Moldovan government would have to pursue membership knowing that it could trigger a new secession crisis. Moscow would gain a means of obstructing accession through Moldova’s internal politics.

    Russia’s economic leverage in Transnistria has weakened, with Gazprom’s direct supplies stopping in January 2025, while the EU accounted for 76.9 per cent of the region’s exports in the first half of 2026.

    A settlement of the kind reported would offer Moscow a means of converting that weakening material leverage into a lasting role in Moldova’s constitutional order. 

    Read more

    [Interview] ‘Whenever we take pro-European political decisions, Russia cut or reduced gas supplies’. Moldova energy minister Dorin Junghietu on why Chișinău is betting on diversification

    Moscow has responded with escalating threats. Russia’s deputy foreign minister Mikhail Galuzin warned that Moscow would treat any attempt to force reunification as an act of war against Russia.

    More recently, Russia’s envoy to the OSCE claimed that Chișinău’s fiscal policy toward the region could provoke a new military confrontation. Moscow is treating the extension of Moldova’s fiscal rules as grounds for escalation.

    Gagauzia has no frozen conflict, no separatist army and no line of contact, despite latent tensions. Its inclusion extends the proposal beyond settling the Transnistrian conflict and into restructuring Moldova’s national decision-making.

    A federal settlement granting Moscow-aligned regional leaderships blocking powers over national decisions could extend Russian influence into Moldova’s central institutions.

    Read more

    EU accession of Moldova and Ukraine is alternative to Nato, as Russia draws new Iron Curtain in Europe

    What Europe should do

    Tajikistan was until now the only country in Central Asia to have ratified the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC. And it’s not the only country withdrawing. No fewer than six other countries have notified the UN of their intention to withdraw this year: Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Venezuela, Chad and Nauru.

    Another blow to the court came last week, when Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping issued a joint declaration warning the court not to abuse its jurisdiction.

    Here’s a quick reminder of what the ICC is, and what it isn’t. The ICC was established in 2002. Its job is to investigate and prosecute individuals accused of four of the most serious international crimes: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression.

    The ICC is a court of last resort. It is supposed to step in only when national authorities are unwilling or genuinely unable to investigate and prosecute these crimes themselves.

    Read more

    The clock is ticking: Europe is running out of time to save the International Criminal Court 

    That’s how it came to issue an arrest warrant against Russian president Vladimir Putin in March 2023 over the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied territories to Russia.

    In November 2024, the court issued arrest warrants against Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant. They are accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, including using starvation as a method of warfare.

    Those warrants were made possible by the fact that the ICC can investigate crimes committed on the territory of a member state, even when the alleged perpetrators come from a country that has never accepted its authority.

    It can also exercise jurisdiction when the accused is a national of a member state, or when the UN Security Council refers a situation to it.

    Now, Washington wants to challenge that principle and, more broadly, dismantle the ICC.

    The US is seeking to prevent the ICC from exercising jurisdiction over individuals from countries that are not members of the court, even when the alleged crimes were committed on the territory of a member state.

    Such a change would fundamentally alter the court’s reach. On top of that, the Trump administration is also putting pressure on the ICC and its member states.

    According to Politico, US diplomats have been urging NATO allies to withdraw from the Rome Statute and immediately stop providing material support to the court.

    Read more

    International Criminal Court wins EU’s top human rights prize in defiance of Trump’s sanctions

    We cannot say whether the seven countries that have notified their withdrawal this year have done so because of US pressure. But the timing is noteworthy, particularly in the cases of Venezuela, Chad, Nauru and Tajikistan.

    And then, there are the sanctions. Over the past months, Washington has sanctioned several judges and prosecutors, including the court’s president, Tomoko Akane. In October this year, the United States went a step further and sanctioned the ICC as an institution.

    These sanctions have concrete consequences: restrictions on financial transactions, frozen assets, and bans on entering the United States, among other things.

    According to MEP Chloé Ridel, these sanctions are already affecting the ICC’s work: the prosecutor’s activities have slowed down, and some people have been sidelined from certain cases.

    But can the US actually dismantle the ICC? If fewer countries cooperate, the court becomes increasingly difficult to operate.

    The court still has 125 member states, and the withdrawal process takes time. But its ability to function depends heavily on international cooperation, financial resources and political support.

  • The data confirm that the age of soldiers killed is increasing, as is the fact that they come from poor regions. The highest number died near Bakhmut and Pokrovsk.
  • Recruitment apparently cannot keep pace with current losses: this year, Russia signed up 10 percent fewer men than last year.
  • Map of the day: Dobropillia.
  • Videos of the day: an Abrams tank adapted for modern warfare; a strike on central Zaporizhzhia; Russians built scaffolding around facilities at a refinery in Perm; it apparently did not help.

    • Two weeks ago, we wrote about data that Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers had stolen from Russia’s statistical agency, Rosstat. The data concerned deceased Russian citizens from 2021 to the end of August 2026.

    From these data, both groups concluded that between 400,000 and 450,000 Russians had been killed in the war. It was still not clear, however, whether the data were authentic — Russian sources had previously also published similar leaks claiming enormous, and therefore implausible, Ukrainian losses.

    However, the hacker groups Cyber Partisan and Silent Crow provided the data to various media outlets. They are now freely accessible to the public (the files total 365 gigabytes).

    It was awaited what the Russian independent website Mediazona, which has long searched for and catalogued the deaths of Russian soldiers through obituaries, official documents and other sources, would say about the data.

    On Monday evening, the Russian website published its analysis of the data.

    Mediazona’s journalists have no doubt that the Rosstat leak contains authentic data on real people who died in the war. They compared it with their own data. They found 95 percent of “their” soldiers in Rosstat’s records.

    “We are convinced that these data are authentic: they were verified using a list of the names of the deceased, including records not previously published, the register of inheritance proceedings, other leaked records from civil registry offices, the texts of court rulings from publicly available sources, and data previously published by Rosstat itself,” Mediazona wrote.

    The analysis of these data suggests that the total number of Russian soldiers killed is even higher than previously estimated.

Its findings also show that some doctors upload sensitive patient data to commercial AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini without approval, and that hospitals struggle to comply with overlapping EU rules on privacy and AI.]]> Hospitals depend on AI they do not control, while EU-funded health startups rarely reach public hospitals in Europe, a report published on Tuesday (24 November) reveals.

    Its findings also show that doctors facing burnout often upload sensitive patient data to commercial AI chatbots without approval, and that hospitals struggle to comply with overlapping EU rules on privacy and AI.

    The EU previously identified healthcare as one of 10 strategic sectors to boost European competitiveness. “I wanted to find out if the EU’s ambitions around scaling health AI and developing truly sovereign European health AI tools really hold up in practice,” lead researcher Júlia Keserű told EUobserver in an interview. 

    Her analysis was run in partnership with Liberties, a human rights watchdog, and was supported by The Collaborative for AI in the Public Interest, a philanthropic project by eBay’s founder.

    The research included interviews with more than 50 hospital workers, scholars and patient advocates, whose insights exposed the struggle of the health sector to comply with EU rules on data privacy and artificial intelligence.

    “There are too many rules and they are too complicated,” Keserű said, explaining that hospitals struggle to comply with rules that are often overlapping and contradictory.

    And while the privacy rights researcher calls for “harmonisation” of rules, she warned that “if simplification means cutting baseline protections for patients, it creates new risks.”

    ‘Careless’ use of AI by stressed doctors

    Among the concerns raised by Keserű’s interviewees, the most prominent was the use of ‘shadow AI’, where clinicians paste potentially sensitive patient data into commercial generative AI tools such as ChatGPT or Gemini without approval from their employers.

Opposition leaders accuse them of brazenly rewriting the rules to shut out hostile voters before the next election. ]]> Slovakia’s parliament voted on Tuesday (24 November) on a proposal that would abolish voting by post for its citizens living abroad in parliamentary elections, replacing it with in-person voting at Slovak embassies and consulates.

    In the 2023 elections, almost 59,000 citizens voted by mail, with the current opposition party emerging as the clear winner among them, receiving 62 percent of the votes.

    “Representatives of this coalition had no problem with postal voting for 20 years, until voters made them pay for it in the last election,” Ľudovít Ódor, Slovak MEP for Renew Europe and former prime minister, told EUobserver.

    “Slovaks living abroad are often critical of the current government,” Martin Hojsík, vice-president of the European Parliament and Slovak MEP, told EUobserver. “Which is precisely why this proposal raises serious questions.”

    “It is hard to escape the impression that the governing coalition is not concerned with election security, but rather with who will be allowed to participate in them,” he added.

    The proposal has become controversial not only because of its practical implications for Slovaks living abroad, but also because of the way it has been brought back onto parliament’s agenda – after already failing twice.

    The bill, introduced by prime minister Robert Fico’s Smer-SSD party, had already been removed from the agenda on 16 September and again on 11 November, after neither its sponsors nor the designated rapporteur attended the scheduled debates. Under parliamentary rules, the second failure should have meant that the proposal could not be discussed again for six months.

    “If this amendment is indeed passed, we will take the matter to the Constitutional Court,” Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová, Slovak MEP for Renew Europe, told EUobserver.

    Party-political motives

    As the organisation of elections remains primarily a national competence, EU member states retain discretion over how their citizens exercise their voting rights.

    For Slovak MEPs, it is interesting to see how political parties use these regulations to alter the conditions of political competition and potentially limit the ability of certain groups of citizens to have a say in the direction their country takes.

    “It is clear that this is a politically motivated move,” Miriam Lexmann, a Slovak MEP from the European People’s Party (EPP), told EUobserver.

    Read more

    ‘Manual for autocrats’: how Fico’s rule-of-law breaches put Slovakia in EU sanctions crosshairs

    It is not a new phenomena. For US president Donald Trump, mail-in ballots represent a “massive voter fraud”, he claimed. And Fico’s coalition has also echoed this argument.

    “Trump has claimed that the most recent US elections were manipulated because of postal voting. But there is absolutely no evidence to support these allegations,” Rasťo Kužel executive director at Memo98, international organisation in the field of media and elections, told EUobserver.

    Many other EU democracies such as Germany use postal voting.

    For Kužel, it is a way of dividing the population.

    In this case, “Smer is positioning itself against people who live abroad. This is primarily about further polarising society.”

      <description><p>Administration is suggesting an added 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total to about 40%</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/25/donald-trump-jensen-huang-nvidia-pardon-senate-hearing-iowa-abdul-el-sayed-latest-news-updates">US politics live – latest updates</a></p></li></ul><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a> is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that would go into effect early next year, the office of the US trade representative said on Wednesday.</p><p>The administration is <a href="https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/november/ustr-makes-determinations-and-proposes-actions-14-section-301-investigations-relating-structural">proposing</a> an additional 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total tax to about 40%. Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/trump-new-china-tariffs-europe">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Judge blocks Brendan Carr-led FCC from taking any further action against ABC’s licenses</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/brendan-carr-fcc-abc-licenses</link>
      <description><p>Federal judge Loren L AliKhan grants preliminary injunction in ABC’s favor after network sued FCC in August</p><p>The federal judge Loren L AliKhan on Wednesday granted a preliminary injunction blocking the Brendan Carr-led Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from taking any action curbing ABC’s ability to renew its broadcast licenses, after the network <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/18/abc-sues-trump-federal-communications-commission">sued the agency</a> in August over an unusual demand to apply early to renew the eight local licenses for stations it owns.</p><p>The FCC claimed that the early renewal process was necessary to procure documents related to an ongoing Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) investigation, but the network countered that it was being punished for editorial coverage that was deemed critical of the Trump administration. The FCC’s order came after Donald Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, criticized ABC for a comment made by the late night host Jimmy Kimmel.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/25/brendan-carr-fcc-abc-licenses">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Oligarchs believe they’re untouchable – the blue wave offers hope that the rampant corruption of the Trump era may soon be over</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/nvidia-staff-what-do-you-think-jensen-huang-return-chief-executive">Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive?</a></p></li></ul><p>One can imagine high-fives all around Nvidia’s boardroom after the board <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/23/jensen-huang-reinstated-as-nvidia-chief-executive">reinstated</a> Jensen Huang to the CEO suite. The market gave the move a fat thumbs-up, boosting Nvidia’s share price by about a third. Shareholders, whose interests the board is meant to represent, are surely happy.</p><p>But like Fifa’s controversial decision to defer the one-match suspension of US forward <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/jul/06/folarin-balogun-red-card-reversal-trump-calls-fifa-explainer">Folarin Balogun</a> after receiving a red card for a foul on Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tarik Muharemović during the World Cup over the summer, Huang’s absolution might backfire.</p><p>Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter <a href="https://eduardoelreportero.substack.com/">Being There</a> on Substack</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/trump-nvidia-gilded-age">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/23/thanksgiving-air-travel-us-explainer</link>
      <description><p>Amid air chaos, travelers will have to navigate an outdated system (and complex company policies if it all goes wrong)</p><p>Millions of people are planning to fly in the US over the Thanksgiving holiday, just two weeks after the US Federal Aviation Administration’s 13 November <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/faa-ground-stop-flights-explained">ground stop</a> halted all flights nationwide for the first time since 9/11 (aside from a brief halt in 2023).</p><p>In the chaos that ensued, some travelers embarked on <a href="https://www.reddit.com/r/royalcaribbean/comments/1xvkopq/comment/19smxjywidlcw/?context=3">overnight drives</a> to catch cruise ships and <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/women-stranded-faa-ground-stop-buy-ford-bronco-27-hour-road-trip-rcna609629">bought new cars</a> to make business meetings. Many had to simply cancel their plans and incur the costs that came with it. More than 18,000 flights were cancelled at a potential cost to travelers of $1.9bn in lost time and related expenses, <a href="https://www.andersoneconomicgroup.com/analysis-nationwide-ground-stop-cost-travelers-nearly-2-billion/">Anderson Economic Group estimates</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/23/thanksgiving-air-travel-us-explainer">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 26 Nov 2026 07:57:50 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[There are two main messages for Ireland in Trump’s latest tariff announcement]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/ireland-and-its-pharma-sector-remains-in-donald-trumps-spotlight/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/ireland-and-its-pharma-sector-remains-in-donald-trumps-spotlight/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 05:21:00 +0000Companies selling to the US market will be going through the detail of the latest tariff announcement from the White House. The devil is always in the fine detail with tariffs, but the 15 per cent cap agreed with the European Union as part of the deal reached last year will remain, meaning for many exporters the impact should be limited at most.

It appears that pharma exports from Ireland – which face no tariffs – will remain excluded. The White House has done deals with the big pharma companies involving more investment in the US. It may be early January before there is full clarity on all sectors.

There are two main messages for Ireland. One is that Donald Trump is sticking to his US tariff policies, despite his midterm elections loss, which was due, in part, to the inflationary pressures these created.

The United States supreme court ruled in early 2026 that many of the tariffs Trump had imposed were illegal. He found a temporary workaround this year and set in train a so-called section 301 investigation of unfair trade practices in trading partners. This was designed to give legal weight to permanent tariffs, without recourse to Congress.

Having “found” what it was looking for in terms of allegedly unfair practices, the latest tariff announcement followed. Whether it is all legally sound remains to be seen.

The second thing to note is how often Ireland is mentioned in the document of findings against the EU. As the EU country with the second highest trade surplus with the US in 2025 – after Germany – Ireland is front and centre in the report, which points to the State’s long record of attracting US investment and promoting exports. In the world of Trumpenomics, having a trade deficit with another country is seen as “losing” and being taken advantage of.

Noting Ireland’s $102.1 billion (€93 billion) exports of pharma drugs and medicines to the US last year, the report warns of the risks it believes this creates for the US. If any disruptions hit the market for these vital products, the US could face shortages or delays, which “would threaten the US health industry and consumers”.

It is not clear what this means for future policy. But Trump’s White House clearly remains perturbed by Ireland operating as an offshore hub for US pharma.

]]>Mark Schiefelbein<![CDATA[‘Trojan horse’ Wesley College development to go ahead despite neighbour objections]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/sports-pitch-development-in-south-dublin-private-school-raises-local-concerns/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/sports-pitch-development-in-south-dublin-private-school-raises-local-concerns/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000A “Trojan horse” development of all-weather rugby and hockey pitches on the grounds of Wesley College, a private school in south county Dublin, is to go ahead despite more than 10 neighbours raising concerns that its “possible consequences are not known, or even hinted at” by the school.

While multiple local residents described the school as a good neighbour and said they would not want to impede the sports facilities on offer to pupils, they objected to the proposal over its scale and potential noise disturbances, among other issues.

Wesley College’s board of governors was granted planning permission by Dún Laoghaire Rathdown County Council in early November for the project, comprising the construction of an all-weather rugby pitch and the refurbishment of an existing hockey pitch to upgrade it to an all-weather multi-sport surface with an 8m-high ball-stop fence and net.

These are to be located on the eastern side of Wesley College’s grounds, “part of the college’s established sports facilities” including grass fields, hockey pitches and tennis courts, according to a planning report supporting the school’s application.

A proposal for six LED floodlights on the rugby pitch was included in the initial planning application, however the council mandated in its decision that these be subject to an additional application.

The Methodist-ethos school, which charges €8,125 for a day pupil to attend this academic year, has come under criticism by local residents for the “gradual erosion” the development may cause to their residential amenity. They all have a Dublin 16 address on Clonard Drive, which runs along the school’s eastern boundary.

“While we recognise the importance of providing sporting facilities for students and the wider community, we have significant concerns regarding the nature, scale and impact” of the proposal, a pair of residents wrote in a letter to the council’s planning office.

“Increased noise from sporting activities, coaching sessions and spectators” will lend itself to “disturbances to nearby residents”, they continued, as well as the “gradual erosion of residential amenity”.

Another couple, four doors down, took issue with the ball-stop fence and net blocking their and their neighbour’s views of the Dublin Wicklow Mountains.

“Such a setting warrants great sensitivity and condensation”, they wrote, and “this unique environment and open outlook is enjoyed by the occupants of around 60 houses on [the road] and has been an established feature of these houses for over 50 years.”

They questioned the need for such a tall fence, too. “While we confess to knowing little about hockey, we would question why it is necessary to have a combination of rigid ball-stop fence and nets at each end of the pitch”.

“Surely, a principal rule of field hockey is to keep the ball at a safe, low level,” they added.

Their next-door neighbour furthered that argument in his letter to the council: “I don’t understand the need for such a high fence, both rigid and netting, if it is only for hockey, which I thought was played close to ground level, except for the odd miscue,” he wrote.

“I hope the size of the fence is not in anticipation of the introduction of other sports, eg Padel. Padel courts are currently in vogue and highly lucrative. Reading the printed word, the impact of a Padel court is very disruptive and, with floodlights, could continue late into the evening,” he continued.

He and his family have lived behind Wesley College for more than 40 years, according to his letter, and the school has been an “excellent” neighbour throughout this time. However, the noise coming from its current hockey pitch, on the western half of campus, “is quite loud, even with the windows closed”.

“It is possible to hear [an] individual shouting instruction and occasionally foul language,” he wrote. “I dread to think what it would be like if the pitch was adjacent to the back of my garden.”

Wesley College Dublin declined to comment on the construction of the new rugby pitch and the refurbishment of the existing hockey pitch. It did not respond to a request for comment on objections to the development.

]]>Dara Mac Donaill<![CDATA[Asian stocks rally in Asia, US tariffs not as dire as feared]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/26/asian-stocks-rally-in-asia-us-tariffs-not-as-dire-as-feared/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/26/asian-stocks-rally-in-asia-us-tariffs-not-as-dire-as-feared/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 07:13:51 +0000Share markets cobbled together a rare rally ‌in Asia on Thursday as the latest salvo of US tariffs looked less damaging than first feared, while the Thanksgiving holiday offered a welcome break from the AI pain trade.

White House proposals for ​new tariffs on 14 major trading partners including China, Japan and the European Union sprang no nasty surprise and, crucially, will not stack on top of those imposed in July. The new rates are also unlikely to be imposed until February or March.

“The macro impact from this increase is likely to be modest, particularly given the fact that the investigations have been telegraphed well in advance,” said ​analysts at JPMorgan.

“Several key imports are still exempt from tariffs, including tech goods, and the administration has shown itself to be sensitive to market disruptions,” they added. “This sensitivity should limit the severity of tariff increases ⁠going forward.”

European EUROSTOXX 50 futures responded by climbing 2.3 per cent, while DAX futures gained 2.1 per cent and FTSE futures added 1.4 per cent.

In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei gained 1.6 per cent, while South Korea’s ‌main ‌index ​rose 1.9 per cent and Taiwan added 1.4 per cent. Any bounce was welcome given Japan is down 8 per cent for the month, while South Korea has shed 16 per cent and Taiwan 15 per cent.

Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rose 1.8 per cent, though Chinese blue chips struggled to make progress.

S&P ⁠500 futures added 0.7 per cent and Nasdaq futures rallied 1.1 per cent, having come back ​from sharp early losses during the previous session.

Tech giant Nvidia remained a source ​of unease after S&P put its credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade citing weaknesses in the chipmaker’s management and board.

Nvidia stock ended down 3.9 per cent at $149.30 on ‌Wednesday, a staggering $2.3 trillion short of its October peak of $243.37.

Bond investors are wondering if the broad losses in global stocks this month coupled with doubts about the durability of AI-driven ⁠business investment might temper the hawkishness of central banks.

It was notable that ⁠Treasury yields hit multi-week lows on Wednesday ​even as US economic growth for the third quarter was revised up sharply to 4.3 per cent, while the Federal Reserve’s favoured measure of core inflation hit an uncomfortably high 3.3 per cent.

While futures imply a 98 per cent chance the Fed will raise rates by 25 basis points in December, speculation of a half-point increase has faded.

Yields on 10-year paper were off at 4.848 per cent, having touched an 11-week trough overnight.

Still, the prospect of extra tariffs was not exactly helpful to the outlook for inflation.

“The latest US tariff announcement is not as alarming as it looks, and the increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we’ve been assuming,” said Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics.

“The additional tariff burden is ‌likely to be small, but will still ⁠provide a marginal boost to prices and keep core goods inflation firm into next year.”

In currency markets, the dollar’s recent strength was tempered somewhat by the drop in Treasury yields, with the dollar index easing a touch to 103.79.

The safe-haven Swiss franc was a major gainer ‌as the dollar eased to 0.8318 francs, while the euro steadied at $1.0965 from its recent low of $1.0881.

The dollar flatlined on the yen at 159.15, with the risk of intervention keeping 160.00 resistance ​intact.

In commodity markets, oil prices held firm after Yemen’s Houthis said they had attacked Saudi Arabia’s largest oil refinery, raising ​concerns about unexpected Middle East supply disruptions.

Brent futures rose 0.7 per cent to $95.25 a barrel, while US crude futures added 0.6 per cent to $84.32 a barrel.

Non-interest-bearing gold firmed 0.2 per cent to $3,589 an ounce, having fallen over 7 per cent so far this month to hit one-year lows. - Reuters

]]>Kiyoshi Ota<![CDATA[Oil rises on supply concerns as Iran claims mine strikes on ships ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/26/oil-rises-on-supply-concerns-as-iran-claims-mine-strikes-on-ships/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/26/oil-rises-on-supply-concerns-as-iran-claims-mine-strikes-on-ships/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 07:08:21 +0000Crude oil prices rose on Thursday, extending gains ‌from the previous session on supply concerns after Yemen’s Houthis said they had hit Saudi Arabia’s largest oil refinery and at ‌least two ships hit Iranian mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude futures were 10 cents, or 0.1 per cent, higher at $94.71 a ​barrel by 0640 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 31 cents, or 0.4 per cent, to $83.99 a barrel. There will be no settlement for WTI on Thursday due to the US Thanksgiving holiday.

Prices rose for the third straight session on ​Thursday and are up about 5 per cent this week, after plunging by around a quarter in the three weeks since the beginning of ⁠November. Middle East exports have been increasing despite continued attacks on shipping, which triggered expectations of ‌a ‌global ​oil surplus this year.

Brent finished 3.5 per cent higher in the previous session, while WTI climbed 2 per cent after Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said they had attacked Saudi Arabia’s Ras ⁠Tanura oil refinery and Riyadh’s financial district.

The ​refinery, Saudi Arabia’s largest, is part of a ​complex that also serves as a major export terminal for Saudi crude, and analysts expect the latest Houthi ‌attacks to increase the geopolitical risk premium.

At ​the same time, shipping has been disrupted through the Strait of Hormuz, where oil supply had ⁠been recovering to near pre-war levels.

An oil tanker ⁠hit a naval ​mine and caught fire in a “restricted zone” in the strait on Wednesday, the semi-official Fars news agency cited an Iranian Army statement as saying. That report came after state media said two oil tankers struck mines and exploded in the strait on Wednesday.

“The broadening of the Middle East conflict threatens to halt the recovery in oil flows in recent weeks. Persian Gulf crude exports rose last week but remain on a declining trend,” said ANZ analyst ‌Daniel Hynes.

OPEC+ ministers will ⁠hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide on their 2027 output policy, facing the challenge of balancing output with the United Arab Emirates no longer ‌in the group, and with Iraq and Kazakhstan pressing OPEC+ to raise its estimate of their oil production capacity.

In the US, ​crude stocks rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in ​the week ended November 20, the Energy Information Administration said, also supporting prices as analysts had expected a 1.5 million-barrel rise. - Reuters

Vásquez<![CDATA[Barclays advances plan to move EU hub to Paris]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/barclays-advances-plan-to-move-eu-hub-to-paris/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/barclays-advances-plan-to-move-eu-hub-to-paris/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Barclays’s plan to move its EU hub from Dublin to Paris moved up a gear this week.

The UK banking group has merged its Irish unit, Barclays Bank Ireland, with a French subsidiary, Barclays ADF, and the enlarged company has been converted into a Societas Europaea, a type of public limited-liability company that can be easily moved from one EU state to another, and renamed as Barclays Europe SE.

The unit now plans to apply to the Irish Companies Registration Office for the transfer of its office to Paris. The move remains subject to various approvals, including the European Central Bank, but is expected to be completed in the first half of 2027.

Barclays revealed in August 2023 that it was weighing moving its fledgling EU headquarters from Ireland to France, less than five years after it chose the Irish capital as its European hub as a result of Brexit. The Irish unit is the fourth-largest bank in the State by assets, at €132.4 billion as of the end of last year.

]]>Nathan Laine<![CDATA[Can my brother move into our elderly father’s house before our inheritance is finalised?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/can-my-brother-move-into-our-elderly-fathers-house-before-our-inheritance-is-finalised/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/26/can-my-brother-move-into-our-elderly-fathers-house-before-our-inheritance-is-finalised/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Q: A reader and his two siblings are to inherit their father’s home and savings in equal shares; he has told them so. The siblings are in agreement with a brother’s plan to move into the house when he retires and their father has died. He would buy out the other two. But could the brother move in now, settling up with his siblings later from the proceeds of the will?

“If this person was in my consultation room, the very first priority is to go home and find the insurance policy,” says Andrea Clarke, principal solicitor at Coyne Solicitors.

“If the property isn’t insured and it burns down, there is no asset,” says Clarke.

The insurer will need to be informed that the house is unoccupied.

The reader’s father was an organised man. As well as sharing his will with his children, he registered an enduring power of attorney (EPA). The reader is the trusted person he appointed to make decisions on his behalf.

This EPA is now being enacted, the reader says. But the EPA alone may not give his son the power to rent out the property or allow his brother to move in.

My mother got an inheritance and a gift from her parents – can she reduce her tax bill?

“Your obligation first and foremost is to carry out the father’s wishes in his will and under the EPA,” says Clarke.

The primary concern should be their father’s care now.

“There is no entitlement for the children to have the house until the father passes away.

“You can’t make decisions in relation to the house or give it to a brother unless the EPA explicitly permits that,” says Clarke.

The reader may need to get court approval to move forward, says Clarke.

If the court did allow the property to be transferred to the brother, capital acquisitions tax (CAT) and capital gains tax would all have to be dealt with now, she says.

Revenue won’t wait until the father dies to be paid the tax.

If the father is availing of the Fair Deal scheme, where his income and assets contribute to paying for his nursing home, the HSE will have a say too, says Clarke.

The HSE might be quite happy for it to be rented, maximising their return. New rules, however, mean tenancies now run in rolling six-year cycles. A tenancy can only be ended mid-cycle on very limited grounds.

“The death of their father would not be a reason to terminate a lease mid-cycle,” says Clarke. This means the siblings may not get vacant possession of the house when they want it.

Renting it on Airbnb, if the EPA and local planning rules allow it, would be more flexible, but it would entail work.

I’m giving my son a €490,000 property. Can I cut tax bill by giving part of it as a loan?

Another option is to rent the house to the brother, but it would have to be at market rent, says Clarke.

Alternatively, the brother could move into the house under a “caretaker’s agreement”, effectively providing a service to the family by occupying the property, says Clarke.

This would have to be carefully drafted so as not be interpreted as a tenancy that could cause problems if the siblings were to fall out.

The caretaker’s agreement would need to address any EPA or court requirements. The HSE, however, may not want someone living in the property for free when renting it would generate income.

If the brother does move under a caretaker’s agreement, he could then seek dwelling house relief – this would allow him to inherit the house tax-free, without using up his tax-free CAT threshold, says Clarke.

He would need to live in the house as his main residence for the three years immediately before his father’s death and have no beneficial interest in another property, and he must live in the house for six years after he has inherited it, to claim the relief.

Can we continue renting to our Ukrainian friends and reclaim our holiday home later?

“The will says everything gets divided between the three of them, but all the beneficiaries could agree that one brother gets the house and the other two get the money,” says Clarke.

An equalisation payment may need to be made here too.

“Making a really well written caretaker’s agreement allowing the brother to go into the property now and taking the subsequent steps could potentially be the most tax-efficient thing for them to do,” says Clarke.

]]><![CDATA[Tech sector is trapped by its own cult of personality]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/11/26/tech-sector-is-trapped-by-its-own-cult-of-personality/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/11/26/tech-sector-is-trapped-by-its-own-cult-of-personality/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 05:55:00 +0000Look in my eyes, what do you see? Thus Corey Glover begins Living Colour’s 1988 classic Cult of Personality. The opening guitar riff drags your attention from whatever you are doing and demands your focus.

The song dives into the faith that ordinary people are willing to put into charismatic individuals, irrespective of ideology or moral stance. It was partially inspired by Khrushchev denouncing Stalin in 1956, but also makes reference to Gandhi and JFK.

In related news, Jensen Huang is back as chief executive of Nvidia after being out of his job just long enough to finish GTA VI.

Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993, has returned to the job after an extraordinary fortnight. His resignation on November 12th followed revelations about extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The other allegations related to staff members of Nvidia.

These are normal reasons to resign or be ousted. That goes for the vast majority of people in leadership positions in companies of all sizes globally, let alone the boss of a company upon which the artificial intelligence (AI) sector is dependent.

Almost immediately, calls came for Huang to be reinstated. Elon Musk and Donald Trump were among the loudest advocates. On November 17th, Nvidia’s board said he would not be reinstated. By Monday, November 23rd, that had all changed and he was back in the top job.

The market loved the news, Nvidia’s share price rose by 31.5 per cent on Monday after plummeting in the week and a half following his resignation. While the price has bounced back, it is still considerably down on when news of Huang’s indiscretions were first revealed.

Look out Ireland, nothing says AI bubble quite like the return of Jensen Huang

That the price can swing so wildly based on the whims and actions of one man is not healthy. Huang is one of a long line of tech leaders who have been elevated in importance above the institution they lead.

In simple terms, Jensen Huang has become an existential necessity for Nvidia.

It’s somewhat apt that at a time of discussions about AI replacing humans in more and more facets of work and life, that the boss of the most important AI company is deemed irreplaceable.

Automation is meant to be capable of replacing quite a lot of the duties in management and tech roles, yet this tech company can’t manage without a 63-year-old that loves his leather jacket.

We’re far beyond debates of right and wrong or what is fair. This is a matter of an industry making itself needlessly fragile.

Think of the corporate governance implications of this. The board of Nvidia has essentially shown itself to be incapable of keeping out an individual who is a walking example of someone that should be kept as far away from the business as possible.

Even allowing for the pressure that can be exerted by the US president, this fixation on a single figure is a recipe for disaster across the sector.

US stocks sell-off deepens as AI trade cracks

That Huang’s initial departure could cause such a mighty downward swing in Nvidia’s stock should alarm the whole industry. The partial, but far from total, rebound upon his return is just as concerning.

Moving on from a founder boss isn’t easy, yet it can be done. Apple took the mildest of early hits to its share price when Tim Cook replaced Steve Jobs, granted that was the second run of Jobs in the top job. Microsoft’s share price actually went up notably after Steve Ballmer replaced Bill Gates.

Donald Trump proposes raft of new tariffs on major economies

Yet those were planned continuity switches. The plan for Nvidia seems to be to trust that Huang will live forever.

It’s far from alone. Mark Zuckerberg is essentially unsackable at Meta, Elon Musk is in similar if not quite so invulnerable a position at both Tesla and SpaceX.

In the case of either having to depart due to unforeseen circumstances, who steps in as the boss is far from obvious. We’ve already seen this when Sam Altman had to essentially be his own replacement at OpenAI in 2023 as his dismissal by the board led to a revolt from staff.

That goes across the board in the sector as it currently stands. It doesn’t have to be this way, Uber survived the sudden and explosive departure of Travis Kalanick. Bill McDermott’s departure at SAP was in no way controversial but it was extremely sudden, yet SAP still managed fine.

Now, more than ever, the tech sector is trapped by its own cult of personality. Investment has always been about people more than products, but the Jensen Huang situation has taken this to extremes.

A cult of personality isn’t just about the person being worshipped but about the people willing to do the worshipping.

The market is at a point where it doesn’t trust multitrillion dollar companies with tens of thousands of highly skilled employees to function without the one true leader.

Vibes and pixie dust seem to be the foundations of the industry as it stands.

The reader’s situation is the reality facing many children who grew up in Ireland but now find themselves unable to return here as adults.

The Government’s family reunification policy, which includes visa applications for those wanting to join family members, has narrowed significantly over the past year, particularly for adult children, says Kellie McLaughlin, solicitor with Gibson & Associates.

“It expressly states now that family reunification may only be sought for an adult child over 18 where they are in the care of the parent sponsor – so someone who has a serious medical or psychological condition that makes their independent life unsustainable,” says McLaughlin.

Previously, adult children aged 18 to 23 in full-time education could qualify as nuclear family members but the Department of Justice removed this pathway in the past two years when it tightened rules.

So, even though the reader has spent much of his childhood in Dublin and his parents and sister are here, the rules prevent him from joining them through family reunification.

Seeking permission to live here through study and employment permits are now his best option, says McLaughlin.

To get a student visa as a non-European Economic Area (EEA) national in Ireland, you must get admission to a full-time course listed on the Government-maintained Interim List of Eligible Programmes. You will have to prove you have sufficient funds and submit an online application through the Irish immigration system.

This Stamp 2 visa is granted for one year initially and can be renewed for up to seven years, depending on the course duration. A student’s attendance record and course progression are verified.

The reader could work part-time during his studies but cannot access publicly funded services or receive social welfare payments.

Time spent on a Stamp 2 visa also does not count toward the five-year reckonable residence requirement for Irish citizenship by naturalisation.

After completing his studies, the reader could seek a Stamp 1G “graduate” permission to stay in Ireland. This is usually granted for one year to those completing a degree-level programme and two with a master’s.

Once he receives the Stamp 1G, his time here starts to accrue towards naturalisation, says McLaughlin.

“The 1G gives a pathway to people who qualify in Ireland but who might need some time before they receive a job offer that will meet employment permit criteria,” says McLaughlin.

“It gives them that two-year period to work in any type of employment. It doesn’t necessarily need to be tied to their qualification but, within that time frame, it’s expected that they pursue an employment offer that will make them eligible to apply for either a general employment permit or critical skills employment permit.”

The Government has designed the latter to attract highly skilled workers in areas where Ireland is facing labour shortages, such as doctors, nurses, midwives, ICT and construction professionals.

If the reader gets a critical skills or a general employment permit in Ireland, he will receive Stamp 1 immigration permission. This will allow him to work or operate a business in Ireland under specific conditions.

“Once he has completed two years on Stamp 1, he can then apply for Stamp 4,” says McLaughlin.

This will allow him to live, work or study in Ireland without an employment permit. He can work for any employer and change jobs without getting a new work permit, or he can start a business.

‘I paid tax on earlier gifts from my parent. Will they reduce my €400,000 tax-free limit?’

The reader should bear in mind that there is some discussion at the moment that the five-year period to naturalisation might increase to eight years.

If, however, after getting his graduate permission, he runs into difficulty getting a job that would allow him to move to a critical skills permit, he could then make a discretionary request to the Minister for Justice to allow him to remain in the employment he is in, without being confined to employment permit criteria, says McLaughlin.

“That’s when family circumstances and the fact that he has Irish-citizen family members, would become really important,” she says.

]]><![CDATA[US comedy gag about a sister who quits job to care for dad is no joke]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/26/us-comedy-gag-about-a-sister-who-quits-job-to-care-for-dad-is-no-joke/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/26/us-comedy-gag-about-a-sister-who-quits-job-to-care-for-dad-is-no-joke/Thu, 26 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000

If you didn’t laugh, you may have cried – or maybe you did both – after watching Saturday Night Live’s Sister sketch when it flooded into family and friends’ messaging apps earlier this month.

In the American comedy programme’s skit, a son realises his ageing father needs more care at home but he doesn’t want to put Dad in a nursing home and live-in care could cost thousands.

He says: “I didn’t know where to turn. That’s when I heard about Sister. Sister is a live-in 24/7 eldercare provider that is completely free and also … your sister.

“Signing up couldn’t be easier. Simply text ‘Dad fell’ to Sister and she will quit her job, break her lease and move halfway across the country to take care of him.”

She manages medications, handles doctors, insurance companies and pharmacists, and can even bring her reluctant husband along – all without affecting the son’s 50 per cent share of the inheritance – because the parents’ will predates their dementia. Now, the son says, “I can get back to my life and the stuff I like to do.”

The parody ends with “Quantities are limited. Sister may break down without warning. Offer void if Sister has a good therapist.”

The comedy lands so well because it’s painfully true. “When care intensifies, women’s employment pays the price,” according to the European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE). When care is unavailable, unaffordable or does not meet families’ needs, someone has to fill the gap. Too often, that someone is a woman.

“What may begin as a private decision about how a family organises care can therefore have very broad consequences for employment, income and gender equality,” says EIGE.

Of course, plenty of men look after their parents and children, too. But as care responsibilities intensify over time, it’s women who are substantially more likely than men to leave employment. Lower-income carers, who tend to be women, are most exposed to care-related employment penalties. EIGE says “27 per cent of lower-income carers report reducing working hours or leaving employment due to care, compared with 20 per cent of middle-income carers and 17 per cent of higher-income carers”.

The big squeeze

With an estimated one in nine people in the workforce both caring for a loved one and managing their career, employers need to start future-proofing their employee benefits. The numbers are probably going only one way due to our ageing population but supports, both private and public, are limited.

In Ireland, employer-funded carer supports fall into two main categories: dedicated paid carer leave, which is still rare, and structured, carer-friendly workplace programmes. which are unpaid and more common in large employers.

The State offers limited supports for carers. Under the Carer’s Leave Act, eligible employees can take unpaid leave of between 13 and 104 weeks to provide full-time care to a qualifying person. Employees may qualify for Department of Social Protection payments such as carer’s benefit (PRSI-based) or carer’s allowance (means-tested). There’s also statutory medical care leave of up to five days of unpaid leave in a 12-month period.

Family Carers Ireland (FCI) estimates there are more than 624,000 family carers, and that at least 270,000 are balancing paid work with care. FCI thinks the number of working carers is even higher than that, as many people do not see themselves as carers. They see themselves simply as wives, daughter, sons or neighbours.

When South East Technological University surveyed its staff after joining FCI’s Caring Employers programme, 60 per cent identified as family carers. Most employers simply never ask this question, so the numbers are hard to quantify.

Ibec’s Better Care Better Business report, published in March 2024, gives us a snapshot of what this costs carers who also work outside the home. Of the carers surveyed, 63 per cent were in employment and 73 per cent of those found it challenging to balance work and care. Some 57 per cent reported added financial pressure and more than a third said caring had affected their careers.

Carers are often exhausted and don’t know where to turn for support. While 57 per cent said their employer had been flexible, only 29 per cent were aware of a company policy on caring and just 21 per cent had ever received paid leave for it. Most support seems to depend on company or managerial goodwill.

‘I care for my elderly parents, but my efforts are taken for granted. I think I might be going mad’

FCI’s State of Caring 2026 report, based on responses from 2,930 carers, describes the reality of informal unpaid supports. Some 71 per cent say caring has harmed their health, and the same proportion find it difficult to make ends meet.

When caring responsibilities become unmanageable, employees are often forced to make difficult choices. Some reduce their hours, others take extended leave and many leave the workforce altogether, often permanently. Carers who remain in work report less loneliness than those who have left, which is one reason the charity wants carers kept in employment wherever possible.

Amongst women: Why are there so few men in caring roles?

The cost to employers in recruitment, training and lost institutional knowledge is significant, and it is largely avoidable. Unaddressed caregiving interruptions carry real costs, including an estimated €615 million annually in Ireland from eldercare-related work disruptions alone, says FCI.

Small, practical actions can make a meaningful difference to employees such as offering flexible working options, showing understanding during challenging periods, encouraging open and respectful conversations, providing access to leave and wellbeing supports, communicating information on rights and entitlements through human resources and fostering empathetic leadership.

‘All the caring I put into my parents – the time, effort and money – is gone, wasted’

Employer toolkit

  1. Find out who your carers are. Run an anonymous survey. Most will not volunteer the information and many do not use the word carer.
  2. Write a carer policy and publicise it. If only three in 10 carers know a policy exists, it’s not doing its job.
  3. Train line managers. When flexibility is granted informally, it’s only as good as the next manager.
  4. Offer to pay for some carer days beyond the legal requirement, and ensure that dependents include parents, in-laws and other relatives. Family comes in many shapes and sizes.
  5. Make flexibility two-way. Offer workers compressed or reduced hours with an agreed route back to full hours when care needs change.
  6. Introduce a carer passport so arrangements do not have to be renegotiated after every restructure or new manager.
  7. Provide practical information. In the middle of a crisis, most people first need to understand home supports, the Fair Deal scheme and enduring power of attorney. The local HSE home support office or public health nurse is often the first port of call.
  8. Plan for the carers you will have. With an ageing population, employees who are not carers today will be tomorrow so explore those pathways now.

So, what’s the real cost of the Sister gag? The punchline is that Sister is free. She’s not. The cost shows up in her health, her hours, her reduced pension pot and her lost promotion prospects. Eventually it shows up for her employer too, in turnover and lost experience, when she decides the only way to manage is to leave.

Employers can’t make relatives share the load. But they can stop assuming that someone’s sister – who might also be their best employee – will absorb it.
