]]>South_agency<![CDATA[Spend your way to a holiday: Can the right bank card really get you free flights?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/25/spend-your-way-to-a-holiday-can-the-right-bank-card-really-get-you-free-flights/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/25/spend-your-way-to-a-holiday-can-the-right-bank-card-really-get-you-free-flights/Wed, 25 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Can you turn your everyday spending into holidays? Some credit cards and debit cards offer free flights and travel perks linked to your spending.

If you have some big-ticket purchases coming up in 2027 then putting them on the right card in a planned way could send you on your next holiday.

So which cards will get you flying sooner? How much could you really save on flights? And is chasing rewards like this even worth it?

Rewards

Card rewards are big business in the United States. Card issuers there can charge far higher card fees than those in the European Union, giving them a bigger margin to fund benefits. Many Americans hold multiple cards just to chase the perks.

Although the rewards were once synonymous with glamorous travel, hotel or dining benefits, an equal number of US cardholders are now using their rewards to pay for essentials such as groceries and fuel.

In Europe, using debit cards and bank transfers is more common for everyday spending. Large-scale card rewards programmes are less part of our culture. But there are some credit and debit cards here that trumpet their travel perks, including free and discounted fares, travel insurance, airport lounge access and priority boarding.

Revolut is big on travel perks. Bank of Ireland was too – until last week. It is withdrawing the Aer Card, a credit card it offers in association with Aer Lingus. Aer cardholders could claim two free Aer Lingus flights and earn “Avios”, a loyalty currency used by several major airlines, at an accelerated pace.

Spend your gift vouchers as soon as you get them – there’s no point in waiting

The move follows criticisms about the difficulty in redeeming the Aer Lingus flight freebie.

Getting a free airfare for simply tapping your card feels like a good deal. But choosing a card for its travel rewards alone will be a false economy if the card membership fees, transaction charges, interest and the hassle of claiming your benefits outweigh the perks.

Credit cards in particular are an expensive form of borrowing. They make most sense if you can pay what you owe in full and on time. Setting up a direct debit to clear the full balance will prevent costly interest charges.

So spend within the lines, watch for fees and check for ease of booking and that the travel rewards offered by your card provider may be actual rewards.

The recently discontinued Aer credit card, offered by Bank of Ireland in partnership with Aer Lingus, was all about the travel perks. Examining what was good and bad about this card is instructive.

The sales pitch was that once you hit spending of €5,000 or more in a “reward year” – so in the 12-month period starting from the date the credit card account was opened, you got two free return tickets on an Aer Lingus ticketed and operated service from Dublin, Cork, Shannon or Belfast to Europe.

There were other sweeteners, too: cardholders would automatically get two Aer Lingus “fast track” passes to get you through Dublin and Shannon Airport security, though fast track wasn’t available Cork.

You’d get two free Aer Lingus Lounge passes and two priority boarding passes every year, too. You also got multi-trip travel insurance for a family of four, including winter sports cover.

Bank of Ireland valued these sweeteners at “over €400 a year”.

The free multi-trip travel insurance was a nice touch, but if you had private health insurance, this cover may already be included in your premium, or could be added for a small fee, making this perk redundant.

The Aer Lingus lounge has free sandwiches, snacks, coffees and juices. With food in the main airport costing an arm and a leg, this was arguably a useful perk. But the two passes could make some tough choices on a family holiday as children aged over two needed their own pass.

Two free return Aer Lingus flights to Europe for two people could definitely take the sting out of the cost of a summer holiday, a midterm break trip, a city break with friends or a Six Nations rugby weekend.

The reward flight included a free 10kg carry-on bag, but you still had to pay taxes, fees and charges on the flights. Users say these typically come to about €70 for two return flights.

Aer Lingus says there were just two Aer credit card seats available to book on each eligible flight.

But you couldn’t actually book your free flights through aerlingus.com – you couldn’t directly book at all. Instead, you submit a “request” to a separate credit card portal, specifying all your passenger information and a few different preferred dates.

Once you completed the form, you got a “case number” and an Aer Lingus agent contacted you about your case. So it was not as easy as booking a free flight of your choice.

Reddit users have plenty to say about this. Some describe the free flight request process as a “nightmare” and an “endless loop”.

Some users report it taking three or more attempts, submitting different possible travel dates and several weeks to get flights approved.

Revolut customers can earn RevPoints. These can be converted one to one for “Avios” and redeemed in full or part payment towards flights with partner airlines, including Aer Lingus, British Airways and KLM.

Harvey does that by spending on her Aer card and Revolut card and by converting her Tesco Clubcard points to Avios.

She watches out for promotions that enable 20 per cent more Avios points when converting.

Avios points helped towards a family trip to Florida this year.

This is the most dangerous time for scams with 55 per cent of respondents saying they were more likely to purchase from retailers they had not used before in the run up to Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Christmas than during the rest of the year.

The research found that 69 per cent of consumers were more likely to trust a seller or business if they appeared to be based in Ireland.

“When something feels familiar, local or friendly, our brains take a shortcut and treat it as safe,” chartered psychologist Allison Keating said.

She said fake listings that copied well-known brands or phishing messages that used a supplier’s familiarity were “a mechanism to create trust, things we have encountered before feel safer and the halo effect means that one positive impression spills over into assumptions of honesty”.

Keating said this was known as a truth default. “We assume people are being honest, because everyday life would be unworkable otherwise, but scammers can take advantage of this,” she said.

“Most social norms discourage questioning someone’s honesty, so challenging a person feels rude and the fear of causing offence with that challenge is immediate and vivid while the financial loss feels abstract and unlikely.”

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[The economics of the AI boom are actually quite old-fashioned]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/21/david-mcwilliams-the-economics-of-the-ai-boom-are-actually-quite-old-fashioned/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/11/21/david-mcwilliams-the-economics-of-the-ai-boom-are-actually-quite-old-fashioned/Sat, 21 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000This week saw the largest share offering the world has ever seen. Anthropic, the AI company that makes Claude, floated on the US stock market with an initial value of just over $1 trillion – a thousand billion dollars. Founded only six years ago, it is today the 10th most valuable corporation in the US.

With the share offering coming a week after the Jensen Huang scandal, it seems that the world is captured by some AI story or another. Even global politics is in thrall to this new technology. On Thursday, when Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sat together, it was clear that the new cold war was as much about tech as arms. We are looking at an industrial transformation on the scale of the move to oil and gas in the early 20th century. It will change the world, but that doesn’t mean everyone can profit from it.

Despite all the money flooding into what is known as “the AI trade”, there seems to be precious little understanding of the economics underpinning the AI boom. Where is the money going, why is everything so expensive and what are the risks that it collapses following one big speculative mania?

When so few people have the answers, it makes sense to ask the questions.

The AI story is portrayed as a high-end technology story, but when you drill down a bit, the economics of AI seem close to old-fashioned heavy industry. It involves pouring concrete, connecting power grids and buying manufactured microchips at a large scale. The lion’s share of the money goes on imported hardware. Very little of the spending is creating new tech jobs. And a growing share of the AI buildout – estimated to be $1 trillion this year – is being financed with borrowings that will need to be paid back sooner or later.

Who is profiting at the moment, who is paying, and how long can it last?

Most of the profits are being made by chipmakers largely based in Asia. Most of the cost is borne by the companies in the US doing all the borrowing, those building or renting the data centres. In addition, as almost everything uses chips – your phone, your car and your fridge – we are all paying through higher costs in our data-driven economy. The amount of new debt means the AI boom is dependent on the rate of interest, the patience of lenders and the tolerance of local communities for data centres, which were a big issue in the US midterms, as was a general dislike of the tech titans who dominate the AI world.

A data centre needs four things: chips, land, water and electricity. Building a new facility can take about two years. There’s a lot of concrete to pour. The amount of money, water and electricity required is enormous. Consider a 1 gigawatt (GW) campus of data centres. Granted, this is a huge data centre but it gives us an idea of the scale of the industrial transformation in front of us. One GW of electricity roughly corresponds to the output of a nuclear power plant or the annual electricity for some 650,000 houses – bigger than Dublin. About 10.5 billion gallons of water are needed to cool the machines, about enough for 100,000 households, and it needs around 700-1,100 acres of space, about half the total size of Phoenix Park. Are you beginning to grasp the scale?

There is little indication we have a plan for what to do if the AI bubble bursts

Most data centres are not this big, running on the megawatt rather than gigawatt scale, closer to 100-250MW of energy, but the demands of AI mean this figure is trending relentlessly upwards, which makes it worthwhile to look at the jumbo data centre.

A 1GW data centre costs about $50 billion – roughly $15 billion for the facility and $35 billion for the compute to power it. Chips make up roughly 70 per cent of the total cost. Because chips dominate the cost, the profits flow to whoever makes them. Nvidia and the amorous Jensen Huang may well design these chips, but they do not manufacture them. Rather, the likes of SK Hynix, TSMC and others do, with Korea, Taiwan and Japan controlling manufacturing. Others will want to get in on the game.

AI fever is producing some strange symptoms

The hyperscalers, companies such as Google and Meta, are designing their own chips, elbowing in on Nvidia’s turf. Geo-strategically, rival suppliers, particularly in China, will emerge. Greater supply of chips will bring down the cost and as the cost of chips falls, the price of using AI will fall. The dilemma for companies such as Anthropic is that if the price of using it falls, its revenues will fall, undermining its new position as the 10th most valuable company in the US.

Not only is the industrial model changing rapidly, with new competitors emerging at every stage of the supply chain, but maybe – more critically – the financing of the AI transformation has changed from cash flow to debt and equity. The hyperscalers, such as Google, used to finance their AI businesses from their large cash flow but, as the costs have risen, even a big company such as Google has had to start borrowing money.

About 10 per cent of all global investment-grade bonds are already related to AI, possibly rising to 16–19 per cent by next year. The AI borrower is in a highly competitive market. For example, the US government bond yields roughly 5 per cent with essentially no risk, so every data centre bond competes with sovereign debt.

Moreover, central banks that are trying to bear down on inflation are raising interest rates, pushing up rates everywhere. Markets are already getting nervous. Hyperscalers with other subscription businesses can borrow cheaply, but others such as Oracle are paying the widest spread. There is also another group of AI-related businesses called neo-clouds that offer cheaper data centre services than Google, Meta, Amazon or Microsoft. You might have heard of names such as CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda and Crusoe. They are paying much higher interest to get money and are most exposed to any change in interest rates or market sentiment.

Over the past few weeks, the huge amounts of money involved have put the wind up financial markets. Can the AI companies such as Anthropic that have yet to make a profit generate money to validate their huge valuations? Will the hyperscalers continue to bankroll our datacentres? Will banks start to call in loans? And can all this credit continue to flow into a sector that is spending so much but – at least so far – is earning so little?

We’ve seen boom and bust before. Will this be the biggest one?

]]>imaginima<![CDATA[Tax-free lump-sum loophole for workers is set to close in Finance Act]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/24/tax-free-lump-sum-loophole-set-to-close-in-finance-act/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/24/tax-free-lump-sum-loophole-set-to-close-in-finance-act/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 05:28:00 +0000It has long been the case that workers can benefit from a tax-free lump sum of up to €200,000 throughout their lifetime, and across redundancy payouts and various pension vehicles.

However, a loophole has been in place, which meant some people, either inadvertently or deliberately, have been able to benefit from the tax advantages during both redundancy and retirement.

Now the Government is working on closing this mismatch in the upcoming Finance Act. What will it mean for tax-free lump sums going forward? And how should people plan for a lump sum at retirement?

Finance Bill update

The tax-free lump sum does not have to be received just the once, it can be paid out several times – in a termination payment, different pension pots, etc – but they must reference each other up to the limit of €200,000.

If you opt to avail of it (or some of it) in a termination payment, then you must sign a waiver indicating that you have already availed of it.

However, this waiver is only tied to that current employment – and so if someone was to leave a job, use the lump sum to reduce the amount of tax payable on their redundancy payment, and transfer their pension to a PRSA, then they could once more avail of the lump sum at retirement, because they would no longer be claiming in relation to that old employment, as PRSAs aren’t covered by the waiver.

This situation has been in place since 2002, when PRSAs were created.

“As a result you had a slightly unusual result whereby occupational pension schemes were included when you were calculating pension lump sums that one might receive. But PRSAs were excluded,” says Munro O’Dwyer, a partner with PwC.

It may not have been a big cohort that availed of it. First of all, you would have had to receive a termination payment and the figures would need to have been substantial enough to make use of possible double lump sum.

And many may not realise the impact of having some pension funds in a PRSA.

“People who had previously waived their right to a pension lump sum have inadvertently benefited from this loophole,” says Jim Connolly, head of pensions with Goodbody.

But it’s likely that others may have deliberately availed of it.

“Where it gets a lot more grey is where people took an action to position themselves in PRSAs, to take advantage of this mismatch,” says O’Dwyer.

Given the mismatch – and the possibility for people to avail of it in excess of the lifetime limit – in this year’s Finance Bill there has been a move to close this, by extending the waiver to “the broader suite of modern pension products that are now available”. These include PRSAs, MyFutureFund, pan-European pension products, as well as foreign pension plans.

In that way, the tax relief on offer should be the same to all – regardless of the pension product in place.

Pension or the new investment account: where should your spare cash go?

It is expected that the change will take place from January 1st, 2027, pending enactment of the Finance Bill. So, if you’re calculating something from January 1st, 2027, O’Dwyer says PRSAs will be in scope.

“What’s less clear is for waivers signed historically,” he says.

But the Finance Bill may yet be changed before it is enacted.

How is my lump sum calculated?

If you haven’t accessed some of your lump sum in a redundancy payment – or at least did so prior to the Finance Bill amendment – the maximum tax-free amount at retirement depends on one of two calculations.

Firstly, if it’s a PRSA, it will always be based on 25 per cent of the fund, up to €200,000. A retirement fund of €100,000 would mean a tax-free lump sum of €25,000; a €300,000 fund would mean a tax-free lump sum of €75,000; a €500,000 fund would get €125,000; and €1 million, €200,000 (plus €50,000 to be taxed).

A favourable rate of tax, at 20 per cent, applies on the next tranche of between €200,000 and €500,000. Above that you’ll face your marginal rate of tax. The balance of the fund can then be put into either an annuity or an approved retirement fund (ARF).

This rule also applies to occupational schemes, but there is another way of calculating the tax-free element: the salary and service formula. This depends on how long you’ve worked with your current employer, and your final pensionable salary. If you are eligible this can be 1.5 times your final salary – so can exceed the other calculation. Someone with a pension fund of €150,000 for example, would get only €37,500 based on the 25 per cent calculation but could get the full amount if they had a salary of €100,000.

But it’s not just about how much you earn when you retire, according to Connolly. Revenue applies a “final remuneration” approach to calculating this figure, which means that you can look back over salary history up to 10 years – and take the best average.

The kicker with the salary and service calculation, however, is that you have to buy an annuity with your fund (apart from your additional voluntary contributions or AVCs as they are better known).

If you have a bumper pension pot, and will easily meet the €200,000 tax-free limit, then how you calculate this lump sum won’t matter. What’s more of a concern is how you draw down your pension income via an ARF or annuity.

“For a higher earner it’s not going to cause much of a complication,” says O’Dwyer.

If, however, your fund won’t hit the limit then it needs more attention.

“If you’ve a million euro in your fund – it’s simple, you get €200,000. The challenge is if you’ve €150,000,” says O’Dwyer, noting that someone might want to maximise their tax-free amount via a salary and service calculation – but may not want to buy an annuity.

Pension millionaires to benefit from higher tax relief over coming years

There could be an argument then, to remove the annuity requirement from the salary and service option.

“In some respect, having different options is fine, but prescribing what you do with the balance is where the issue comes in,” O’Dwyer says.

What if I’m in a defined-benefit pension scheme?

According to Connolly, lump-sum planning for those in defined-benefit (DB) schemes can be tricky, as to take a tax-free lump-sum of 1.5 times final salary will reduce the pension payments. This is known as commutation. Those with such a pension plan also have an option of taking 25 per cent of the pension fund if they get a transfer value and move the fund.

But those in DB plans don’t always have the full information to make the best decision. “Trustees generally don’t make them aware they have the option of a transfer value,” says Connolly, noting there can be a “massive difference” between the two ways of calculating the lump sum.

Moreover, someone with a serious illness, for example, may be better to get the transfer value, rather than have their pension paid out in an annuity.

While there is no regulatory requirement to offer a retiree a transfer value, Connolly argues there is a fiduciary one to act in the best interest of members of the DB scheme.

How to plan for your lump sum

“I would have an eye on my lump-sum entitlements from age 50 onwards,” says Connolly.

The age 50 is a pertinent one, as this is the age you may be able to access certain pension pots, such as those from older employments – you don’t have to draw down all your pots at the same time.

“You can have as many retirements as you’ve had jobs,” says Connolly, and you can take 25 per cent each time you draw a pot down – up to the lifetime limit of €200,000.

But there is a complication. If you use salary and service to calculate your lump sum, and only have 20 years’ service, you’ll need to use the uplift approach to get 1.5 times final salary.

But this enhanced scale means “you do have to reference retained benefits” from other pension pots, O’Dwyer says.

]]><![CDATA[Paddy McKillen firm behind luxury Dublin apartment block records €5.5m ‘loan forgiveness’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/31/paddy-mckillen-firm-behind-luxury-dublin-apartment-block-records-55m-loan-forgiveness/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/31/paddy-mckillen-firm-behind-luxury-dublin-apartment-block-records-55m-loan-forgiveness/Sat, 31 Oct 2026 06:00:01 +0000Paddy McKillen and Padraig Drayne’s firm, which developed a luxury Dublin city centre apartment block, in which homes sold for up to €1.8 million, booked a €5.5 million gain from “loan forgiveness” last year.

Broadfield Development Limited, controlled by McKillen and Drayne, secured permission to build the mixed-use commercial and residential development called 55 Lad Lane in 2017.

Construction work started on the six-storey, 25-unit apartment block in 2019. Apartments have been sold individually in the development over the past two years, with the final home in the block sold earlier this month.

New accounts published by the company show it recorded a “provision for loan forgiveness” of almost €5.5 million last year. That helped drive a profit after tax of close to €3.9 million.

The final tranche of apartments in 55 Lad Lane were sold this year. Based on the Property Price Register, one-, two- and three-bed homes were sold at prices ranging between €550,000 and €1.8 million.

Broadfield Development Limited made €12.9 million of turnover from the sale of the apartments last year, compared to €9.2 million in 2024.

Broadfield said its cost of sales in the year totalled €16.9 million in 2025. Allowing for €504,000 of interest charges on debts, the company recorded an operating loss of close to €4.6 million.

But the business swung from that operating loss to an after-tax profit due largely to the loan forgiveness.

It also earned €310,000 in dividends and booked a positive €1 million item described as an “impact of wind-up cost”. At year end it was still sitting on accumulated losses of €9 million.

Sales materials for the apartment project said the project was financed by AIB. Financial statements showed finance was also provided personally by McKillen and a firm linked to Drayne.

The company’s accounts did not clarify if the loan forgiveness was linked to Broadfield Development’s debts with AIB or other finance provided.

A spokesman for AIB said it does not comment on individual customers. A statement issued on behalf of Broadfield Developments Ltd said the loan forgiveness in question “was internal inter-company financing and AIB was repaid in full”.*

Filings by Broadfield Development Limited in August of this year said that five charges held by AIB over the company had been fully satisfied.

In the latest accounts, directors said the company has an intercompany loan from JSC Properties (Holdings) Limited, the McKillen and Drayne firm that sold Jervis Shopping Centre earlier this year, totalling €8.4 million that fell due at the end of 2025.

In addition to that sum, Broadfield also owed €4.2 million to McKillen, €2.25 million to an entity called Garvagh Finance and €1.9 million to Drayne’s firm, Deanscastle Developments. It also owed €659,000 in VAT and to other creditors.

Broadfield Development Limited disclosed back in its 2022 financial accounts that €16.2 million in loan facilities with AIB had expired in September of that year. Directors were in discussions with the bankers about repayment of the debt facilities from the proceeds of property sales, it said.

Last year, McKillen and Drayne’s firm said the amount outstanding to AIB had fallen to €8.5 million by the end of 2024 and they remained in discussions with the bank. The filing added that a further €4.2 million had been repaid from apartment sale proceeds in 2025.

In August 2026, filings by Broadfield Development Limited said all charges AIB held over the company were now fully satisfied.

A note in the accounts said the company has “no plans to carry out any further development” and its directors were planning to wind up the firm.

*This article was amended on November 24th, 2026 to include a statement issued on behalf of Broadfield Developments Ltd

]]><![CDATA[Almost half of employees in Ireland believe they will have to work beyond 65 for financial reasons]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/24/almost-half-of-staff-believe-they-will-have-to-work-beyond-65-for-financial-reasons/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/24/almost-half-of-staff-believe-they-will-have-to-work-beyond-65-for-financial-reasons/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 00:01:00 +0000Almost half of employees in Ireland believe they will have to work beyond 65 with more than 60 per cent fearing they will not have enough to live comfortably in retirement, new research suggests.

The survey of 1,000 employees, conducted for HR consultants SD Worx, found that 47 per cent of respondents believe they will not be able to retire when they would have intended and 48 per cent believe they will have to work beyond what has been the traditional retirement age in many sectors, 65.

Thirty-five per cent of those questioned, rising to 41 per cent among those aged 55 or over, say they would like to work beyond 65 but the average age respondents suggested they would ideally stop working at was 61.

Just over 60 per cent, however, believe they will have to work beyond their desired retirement age for financial reasons with 66 per cent of women expecting to have to do so compared with 58 per cent of men.

Older employees remain “highly engaged with their work,” the research suggests with four in five (80 per cent) of those aged 55 and over saying they have the energy to do their job well and 82 per cent believing their work has purpose or matters. Both measures are higher among over-55s than among younger employees.

Just 43 per cent of employees aged 55 and over feel their organisation supports them in planning for retirement, however, while just 36 per cent of the same group suggest their employers adjust or adapt work or tasks when needed.

Two-thirds of workers fear their pension won’t be big enough to fund their retirement

Under the Employment (Contractual Retirement Ages) Act 2025, those with a contractual retirement age below 66 can now notify their employer that they wish to stay in work until the State pension age, but the number of people working beyond 65 has already quadrupled to more than 133,000 over the past 25 years with housing and changing family circumstances repeatedly cited as key factors.

“The gap between when people would like to retire and the reality of when they expect to stop working raises important questions for employers,” said Eimear Byrne, managing director at SD Worx Ireland.

“Living longer can mean a retirement that’s almost as long as the average person’s working life. While that is, of course, good news, it does mean that many of us will be working longer out of financial necessity.

“Businesses must think about how they prepare for an ageing workforce and support employees whose retirement plans may change. This means planning ahead, having open conversations about future working arrangements and considering how roles, hours or responsibilities might adapt over time,” she said.

]]>Martin Barraud<![CDATA[Pepper Ireland loans under management down 27% in three years as portfolio sales slow]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/pepper-ireland-loans-under-management-down-27-in-three-years-as-portfolio-sales-slow/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/24/pepper-ireland-loans-under-management-down-27-in-three-years-as-portfolio-sales-slow/Tue, 24 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000Pepper Advantage Ireland, the mortgage services provider used by banks and investment firms, has seen its assets under management decline by 27 per cent to €18 billion in the past three years, driven by borrowers paying down debt following a wave of loan portfolio sales after the 2008 financial crash.

The latest set of accounts for Pepper Finance Corporation (Ireland), the registered name of the business, show that assets under management (AUM) declined by 12 per cent last year, contributing to a 5 per cent decline in revenue, to €64.5 million.

“AUM naturally fluctuates as existing portfolios run down and new mandates migrate to the business. Pepper continues to take on new mandates and expects AUM to grow in 2027,” the company said in a statement.

Pepper Advantage Ireland’s chief executive Niall Sorohan told The Irish Times in May it was developing new lines of business to diversify as the post-crisis era of large non-performing portfolio sales fades.

This includes a new business – called Harbour Credit – aimed at managing unsecured consumer credit for banks, utility firms and semi-State agencies. The company subsequently agreed in July to buy Dilosk, the owner of the ICS Mortgages business, for an undisclosed price.

ICS has a portfolio of €1.7 billion of loans. The deal has not yet been completed.

Pepper rate hike to heap more misery on distressed borrowers

It is expected that Pepper Advantage Ireland will take over servicing the ICS loans from the lender’s current provider, BCM Global. The ICS brand will continue after the deal goes through.

“Pepper Advantage remains Ireland’s leading credit management business, supporting approximately 115,000 residential and commercial loans. 2025 marked another year of positive performance as we continued to invest in the business, and that work has carried through 2026 as we increasingly diversify our offering,” Sorohan said.

“Banks and investors continue to turn to us for our expertise and specialist services, and we expect to add new mandates throughout 2027.”

The wider Pepper Advantage group was acquired in March 2025 by JC Flowers from Australia-founded Pepper Global. The management team of the Irish unit was last year granted an equity-based performance package that is dependent on the new owners achieving a “future exit event”. The report put an equity valuation on the business, for accounting purposes, at €53.4 million.*

Private-equity exit events can be triggered by everything from a refinancing to a sale of a business. While the company’s accounts refer to an expected exit date of August 2029, it said in a statement this assumption is used for accounting and modelling purposes and does not indicate a planned sale timetable.

The average headcount of the business fell to 509 last year from 524 in 2024. Staff costs dipped to €53.3 million from €55.5 million.

Pepper Advantage Ireland paid a €17.1 million dividend to its immediate parent, Pepper Ireland Finance Holdings, in 2024, following on from a €14.1 million payment made in 2023. However, it did not pay a dividend in 2025.

Pepper Advantage plans to rebrand in January as Continuum Credit Group.

*This article was amended to clarify that the €54.3 million accounting value relates to the company, not the size of the management incentive package

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3449233/">
   <title>Karte zeigt großes Windkraftpotenzial</title>
   <description>In Österreich gelten für das Errichten von Windrädern strenge Regeln. Nicht überall können Windparks gebaut werden. Derzeit sind 1.447 Windräder in sechs Bundesländern in Betrieb. Das Potenzial ist aber noch größer, wie eine neue Karte von „Scientists for Future“ (S4F) und Klimadashboard vom Mittwoch zeigt, die erstmals Daten für jede österreichische Gemeinde ausweist.</description>
   <link>https://orf.at/stories/3449233/</link>

Poland’s defence ministry has announced plans to establish a no-fly zone along the country’s eastern border with the aim of making it easier to shoot down Russian missiles and drones that violate Polish airspace.

Meanwhile, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has again suggested that Poland should be allowed to shoot down Russian missiles that are over Ukraine but heading towards the Polish border. However, the defence ministry acknowledged today that NATO is so far opposed to the idea.

Wiceminister obrony Cezary Tomczyk zapowiedział wprowadzenie strefy zakazu lotów przy wschodniej granicy Polski.

Jak poinformował minister Tomczyk, rozporządzenie trafiło do rządowego zespołu, strefa ma obejmować od kilkunastu do 50 kilometrów przy granicy wschodniej Polski i ma… pic.twitter.com/3xF68uNNRU

— Dariusz Wiewiorka (@darekwiewiorka) November 25, 2026

Speaking on Wednesday at the opening of a new military satellite imaging centre, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced that his department “will request the government to establish a no-fly zone on the country’s eastern border, to ensure Poland’s security”.

Tomczyk acknowledged that, after three Russian missiles struck southeastearn Poland last Friday, NATO had offered support, including the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) to Poland.

“But at the same time, the Polish military must do everything possible to protect our interests here and now,” he added.

The defence ministry recently took one such step by allowing easier identification of objects that can be shot down, said Tomczyk. “The no-fly zone at the state border will be an additional factor supporting the operations of the Polish Air Force.”

 

At a subsequent press briefing, Tomczyk provided more details of the plan. The proposed no-fly zone would stretch for a distance of between “a dozen or a few dozen kilometres from the border”, he said.

“When a Polish fighter pilot knows that an aircraft is entering Polish airspace from Ukraine, is flying at a certain altitude and speed, is entering the no-fly zone and is detected on radar, this constitutes grounds for shooting down such an object…We will also urge NATO as a whole to establish such a rule on the eastern flank.”

The deputy minister said that a relevant regulation had already been submitted and “will be processed in the coming weeks”. He expressed hope that the measures could be in place by the end of December or in early January.

As well as last Friday’s missile strikes, on Monday this week a Russian drone entered Poland from Ukraine and spent a few minutes in Polish airspace. The Polish military had been authorised to fire upon it, but eventually did not do so after it turned back towards the border.

Poland is changing the procedures under which its military can fire upon foreign aircraft, citing the "growing threat from Russia".

Visual identification of targets will no longer be required, with other forms of data to be used instead https://t.co/foCWsBDazH

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 29, 2026

The government’s plans for a no-fly zone were, however, questioned by Mariusz Błaszczak, a former defence minister and now head of the parliamentary caucus of Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party.

Błaszczak noted that current regulations already allow the introduction of a temporary no-fly zone. He suggested that what the government had announced was simply a “cosmetic measure” and asked what “real operational capabilities” it would provide to the military.

Earlier on Wednesday, Bloomberg reported, based on unnamed sources, that Poland had, at a NATO meeting called on Monday to discuss last week’s Russian missile strikes in Poland, asked about the possibility of shooting down Russian missiles that are over Ukraine but heading towards NATO states.

Asked about the issue, Tomczyk said that he could not confirm Bloomberg’s reporting, but noted that discussion of shooting down Russian missiles over Ukraine had been going on for months.

“NATO is not in favour of this in any way,” said Tomczyk, quoted by broadcaster TVN. “If we want to make any decisions that concern the space over Ukraine, it must always be a decision of the entire NATO…Many months ago NATO decided that such a procedure was out of the question. And that’s where we stand now.”

NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System to Poland in response to three Russian missiles striking Polish territory last week.

Hours after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone https://t.co/gudQJsPlQ5

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 24, 2026

On Wednesday morning, before Bloomberg’s report had been published, Sikorski, the foreign minister, was asked during an interview with Polskie Radio about the idea of shooting down missiles over Ukraine before they reached Poland.

“A missile or drone approaching our airspace already poses a direct threat to us, so I believe that shooting [it] down over Ukraine at Ukraine’s request would fall within the definition of self-defence,” said Sikorski. However, he acknowledged that any such policy would need to be agreed by NATO.

As far back as 2024, Poland proposed the idea of shooting down Russian missiles over Ukrainian territory. But it was rejected by NATO, whose then-secretary general, Jens Stoltenberg, said that it would risk NATO “becoming part of the conflict”.

The mayor of Warsaw has refused permission for opposition protests outside the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which was taken over last month by a group of government-backed judges, to continue.

City hall, which is under the control of Poland’s main ruling party, the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), says that the demonstration threatens public safety. However, opposition figures have condemned the decision as “authoritarian” and one of the organisers of the protest has pledged to challenge it in court.

Bum.
Jest zakaz organizacji kolejnej manifestacji przed Trybunałem Konstytucyjnym.https://t.co/Ol8gQxC3A1 pic.twitter.com/bUqAkdojxe

— Tomasz Skory (@TomaszSkory) November 25, 2026

On 30 October, a group of eight judges chosen this year by the government’s parliamentary majority – but five of whom opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has refused to swear in – effectively took control of the TK.

They declared that the tribunal’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, was suspended. Meanwhile, riot police surrounded the court and held back protesters, including Święczkowski himself.

Since then, the demonstrators have maintained a constant presence outside the court, while Święczkowski has also periodically appeared. He and Nawrocki argue that the actions of the eight “usurper” judges are illegal and that Święczkowski remains chief justice.

 

Given the ongoing demonstration in front of the court, the judges currently controlling the TK have used a separate entrance that leads in from the next-door chancellery of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

On Monday this week, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, the judge who has declared herself acting head of the court, arranged a meeting with Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, and the commander of Warsaw police, Krzysztof Ogroński, to discuss the protest.

She argued that, by preventing access to the tribunal, the demonstrators were “violating the constitutional and European standard of the right to a court”.

On Wednesday morning, Warsaw city hall announced that Trzaskowski, who is a deputy leader of Tusk’s centrist KO party, had rejected a request for permission to continue the public assembly outside the TK from the end of November until January.

That latter finding prompted Poland’s deputy interior minister with oversight of migration policy to hail today’s rulings as a victory and endorsement of the government’s tough border policies. It was also described as a groundbreaking moment by a leading human rights organisation.

In 2021, Belarus began encouraging, assisting and, in some cases, forcing tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to irregularly cross into the neighbouring EU states of Poland, Lithuania and Latvia.

Belarus engineered the migration crisis as part of the various “hybrid actions” undertaken alongside its ally Russia with the intention of destabilising countries they regard as hostile.

In response, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia took a variety of measures intended to prevent the entry of irregular migrants from Belarus. In many cases, they carried out so-called “pushbacks”, sending migrants who had crossed the border back into Belarus.

 

On Tuesday, the ECHR announced three sets of rulings on cases brought against Poland, Lithuania and Latvia in relation to actions they had taken against specific migrants who had entered from Belarus.

The European court noted that the migrants had “entered unlawfully” as part of Belarus’s “instrumentalisation of migration”, which it described as a “hostile action” that had  “the intention of destabilising the respondent states or the wider region”.

This “represented a deliberate threat to the state” and “was liable to put at risk its essential functions, including the maintenance of law and order and the safeguarding of its national security”.

The court found that states do have the right to control entry, and even fully close their borders, as well as to “remove a foreign national to the instrumentalising state”, without it automatically being a violation of the human rights convention.

However, the ECHR also deemed that, “before removing an individual in such circumstances, national authorities had an obligation to detect those individuals who would be particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill-treatment”.

That included those who had personal vulnerabilities (such as old age, ill health or a disability) or who would face a threat to their life or serious risk of mistreatment by being returned to Belarus.

In the cases of Poland and Latvia, the ECHR found that they had breached the obligation to undertake such an assessment before returning certain migrants.

Warsaw’s first astronomical observatory open to the public and run by a local municipal institution launched on Sunday.

Its organisers say the facility, with two telescopes allowing safe observation of the Sun and photography of the cosmos, is aimed at astronomy enthusiasts as well as children and young people, who will be able to watch the night sky and participate in recording data without needing their own equipment.

The new observatory, which is located on the roof of the Gocław Culture Terminal in the Praga-South of Poland’s capital, was created in response to growing public interest in astronomy, science and new technologies, says city hall.

“Under the three-metre-high dome, specialised equipment awaits, allowing for observation of the sky, including safe viewing of the Sun,” said mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, who visited the facility last week ahead of its official opening.

“Anyone who is interested can come here and learn about space through observation, photographing the sky and hands-on activities,” he added.

The observatory will be free to use but only accessible during organised events, owing to limited space and the expensive equipment it contains, reports newspaper Super Express.

“The dome houses very expensive equipment. For most of the year, it will function as a broadcasting station, and images from the telescopes will be projected onto screens in the main hall of the terminal,” Jacek Białek, head of Gocław Culture Terminal, told the newspaper.

“We will invite people inside the dome as part of programs, the dates of which will be published on the cultural centre’s website,” he added.

Participants in workshops and events will also be able to help collect and analyse data, with Białek noting that the centre will be working closely with scientists from the University of Warsaw

The new facility cost around 500,000 zloty (€111,000), most of which was covered from the district budget, with contributions from private donations as well as grants from the state-owned military optoelectronic equipment company PCO and the national lottery foundation.

 

The core of the new facility is a 14″ DO-GSO (Ritchey-Chrétien) telescope with a mirror diameter of approximately 35 cm and a focal length of approximately 2,850 mm, placed on an EQ8-RH equatorial mount with automatic sky tracking.

This setup, along with a QHY268M Pro monochrome camera, a filter wheel and an electronic focuser, will be used for astrophotography and targeted photometric measurements, producing images suited to Warsaw’s atmospheric conditions.

The observatory also boasts a specialist Sky-Watcher Heliostar 100 H-Alpha telescope, which is used for safe and detailed observation and astrophotography of the Sun, allowing viewers to see structures in the solar atmosphere invisible through an ordinary telescope.

The telescope allows solar prominences – large, bright features extending out from the Sun’s surface – to be observed and compared with images produced on other days. The telescope is protected by a three-metre dome that automatically opens and rotates.

Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector

The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026

The observatory also features a computer coordinating its measurements, a camera showing almost the entire sky, and a weather monitoring system. Observations will depend on atmospheric conditions and visibility.

“Examples of how this telescope might be used include photographing the cosmos and conducting simple research, such as measuring changes in the brightness of stars and producing graphs illustrating these changes,” explained Ewa Konarzewska from Gocław Culture Terminal.

Poland has placed great emphasis on developing its space industry in recent years, with the aim of becoming a major European player in the sector.

Last year, the country launched its first national military satellite. A Polish firm, Creotech Instruments, signed Poland’s largest-ever contract with the European Space Agency, a €52 million deal to build and launch a constellation of Earth observation satellites.

Meanwhile, 2025 also saw astronaut Sławosz Uznański-Wiśniewski become the second-ever Pole to travel into space, as part of an ESA mission to the International Space Station.

Earlier this year, Warsaw was chosen as the location for a new ESA centre focused on civil security and resilience, with the agency’s head declaring that “Poland has rapidly become one of the driving forces in Europe’s space sector”.

A consortium led by FedEx has completed its €7.8 billion (34.5 billion zloty) takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost. The deal will see InPost remain headquartered in Poland, with founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska staying at the helm.

Friday’s announcement brings to a close a process that was first announced in February and received European Commission approval in August. InPost’s shares have now been delisted from the stock exchange.

The takeover follows years of rapid growth for InPost, which pioneered the use of parcel delivery lockers in Poland before spreading rapidly in major western European markets, including France, Spain and the UK.

A consortium of Advent, FedEx, A&R Investments and PPF has completed its takeover of Poland's InPost, which is now private.

InPost has delisted from Euronext Amsterdam. Founder Rafał Brzoska stays on as CEO, and the company remains headquartered in Poland. pic.twitter.com/HWigKVPC3w

— IPO Newsroom (@IPONewsroom_) November 20, 2026

Under the deal, FedEx and Advent, an American private equity firm, each hold 37% of InPost. A&R Investments, Brzoska’s own investment vehicle, has 16% and PPF, a Czech investment fund founded by the late billionaire Petr Kellner, 10%. PPF, A&R and Advent were previously already stakeholders.

The consortium acquired InPost at a price of €15.60 per share, valuing the company at approximately €7.8 billion.

In a statement published on Friday, Advent confirmed that InPost would retain its name, branding, Polish headquarters and operational independence following the takeover. Brzoska, who founded his business in 1999, will continue as CEO alongside the existing management team.

 

“InPost’s home market of Poland will remain the blueprint for new innovations, which will then be scaled across InPost’s wider European network,” said Advent.

They added that the new consortium would now “accelerate investment” in InPost’s operations, helping the firm “extend its reach further”. FedEx and InPost would also “explore opportunities” to cooperate with one another.

“InPost has built a leading position in Europe’s out-of-home delivery segment,” said FedEx’s CEO and president, Raj Subramaniam. “Connecting our global network…with InPost’s last-mile capabilities gives both businesses a potential springboard for profitable growth.”

Brzoska, who is one of Poland’s wealthiest individuals, said that the new partnership would “deliver the long-term capital, global reach and deep technology expertise we require to build on what we have already achieved together as a leading European e-commerce enabler”.

President Macron has thanked Polish delivery giant InPost for its latest investment in France

InPost is the largest operator of parcel lockers in Europe, with around 70,000 across the continent. That includes roughly 30,000 in Poland and 16,000 in the UK, including in branches of the British Post Office, with over 23,000 more in the seven Eurozone countries where InPost operates.

In the second quarter of 2026, InPost had revenue of 4.18 billion zloty (€970 million), up 18.2% year on year, while its number of parcels handled rose 16% to 380.9 million.

Two Ukrainians have been charged in Poland with working on behalf of Russia to paint slogans praising the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist formation responsible for massacring Poles during World War Two, on three monuments in the Polish city of Poznań.

Polish prosecutors say that the operation was intended to fuel hostility between Poles and Ukrainians. The incidents in Poznań were part of a seemingly coordinated wave of similar graffiti on monuments in three other Polish cities.

Ukraińcy malowali na pomnikach hasła „Sława UPA”. Działali na zlecenie wywiaduhttps://t.co/knLgZzo8ct

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 19, 2026

In early November, the words “Slava UPA” (“Glory to the UPA”) were painted in red on three monuments in Poznań commemorating World War Two soldiers.

While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation.

The history of those massacres, and the continued veneration of the UPA by some in Ukraine, has regularly stirred tension between Poland and Ukraine, who are otherwise close allies.

 

On Thursday, the National Prosecutor’s Office confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that two Ukrainians, who can be named only as Nikita S. and Dmytro Y. under Polish privacy law, had been detained and charged in relation to the vandalism.

According to prosecutors, Nikita S., “acting on behalf of Russian intelligence and in order to obtain financial benefit of $500”, persuaded Dmytro Y. to “commit an act of sabotage by painting the slogans” with the aim of “publicly inciting hatred based on national differences between the Polish and Ukrainian peoples”.

The suspects were identified by police and the Internal Security Agency (ABW), who had analysed surveillance footage of the perpetrator, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Both were detained in Poznań, according to PAP.

In the wake of the Poznań vandalism, Poland-based Belarusian news outlet MOST reported that, a few days before the graffiti appeared, an advert offering $500 for someone to paint pro-UPA slogans on monuments in the city had appeared on messaging service Telegram.

When an undercover journalist from the outlet contacted the person offering the job, they were told that similar work was available in other Polish cities.

Around the same time, almost identical graffiti praising the UPA appeared on further monuments in the cities of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Warsaw, including one dedicated to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.

Around a dozen monuments in Poland, including one dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, have been defaced with graffiti glorifying the WWII Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).

Ukraine’s embassy in Warsaw has condemned the vandalism and blamed it on Russia https://t.co/iaZb2CyiPx

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 15, 2026

Last week, local police in Gdańsk confirmed that they had detained a 17-year-old Ukrainian suspected of carrying out the graffiti there and in Gdynia. He has been charged with promoting fascist ideology, incitement to violence and hatred based on nationality, and desecration of monuments.

The Ukrainian embassy in Poland has condemned the acts of vandalism, calling them a “disgraceful provocation” and “a manifestation of the hybrid war that Russia is attempting to wage by any means in European states”.

Poland has been a primary target for Russia’s so-called hybrid actions in Europe, which have included acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and efforts to stir hostility towards Ukrainians.

Such operations are rarely carried out by Russian operatives themselves. Instead, Russia often recruits people already on the ground, often members of Poland’s large Ukrainian and Belarusian migrant communities, as well as Poles themselves in some cases.

In July this year, a Ukrainian teenager was indicted by Polish prosecutors on charges of painting dozens of pro-UPA slogans in public places, including on a monument to victims of the Volhynia massacres.

Defence giant Babcock has secured the backing of Prime Minister Andy Burnham as it landed its largest contract award in history.

The FTSE 100 engineering group has inked a five-year term agreement worth £8.7bn to support the UK’s submarine availability and deterrents at sea.

It is expected to create 3,000 new full-time roles and more than 2,500 apprentice and graduate opportunities for the period, Babcock said.

The contract, dubbed the Gateway Agreement, was signed with the Ministry of Defence and follows on from Babcock’s previous martime support agreement. 

Burnham said the new contract was a “clear demonstration” of the government’s commitment to keep “the public safe”. He added it would protect jobs and help young people into work as well as protect national security. 

A separate Memorandum of Understanding was signed alongside the deal that could take its lifespan up to 15 years, Babcock said. 

Babcock rides high on defence demand

“Babcock will continue to strengthen sovereign, industrial capabilities, bringing benefits to communities across the country, including SMEs and local supply chain. Together we will further strengthen the UK’s defence readiness and national strategic resilience,” the group’s boss Harry Holt said.

The defence firms’ revenue edged up to £2.7bn in the first half of the year, a climb from £2.5bn in the same period last year.

Its contract backlog stood at £8.9bn, while its debt had narrowed to £267m from £351m.

London-listed defence stocks rallied following the Budget, where Chancellor John Healey announced extra funding for defence through the use of public finance institutions (PuFins) at the Budget.

The Chancellor used the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank as a means to borrow cash for defence, without explicitly breaching the government’s fiscal rules.

Healey resigned as defence secretary under Sir Keir Starmer after a row over funds for the Defence Investment Plan. He had demanded a timetable to increase defence spending to three per cent of GDP by 2030, ahead of Nato’s wider target of 3.5 per cent by 2035.

No specific timetable has been set for the three per cent benchmark.

The FTSE 250 firm said it plans to reinvest some of the £8m extra revenue it took during this year’s heatwaves, as record [...]]]>

Halfords has improved its profit target for the second time in a matter of months, as the motoring retailer continues to benefit from a surge in sales during the hot summer months.

The FTSE 250 firm said it plans to reinvest some of the £8m extra revenue it took during this year’s heatwaves, as record temperatures drove demand for seasonal products like camping equipment and cycling gear.

The decision to use this extra proceeds to “accelerate planned investment” will help Halfords reach an underlying pre-tax profit of between £60m and £65m in the full year, the group told shareholders. 

The retailer and garage operator had already boosted its target to a range of £55m and £65m, despite the market initially expecting a return of about £53m. The group is on track to comfortably beat last year’s underlying pre-tax profit of £45m.

The firm notched a £35.5m pre-tax profit in the six months to October, it told shareholders on Thursday, more than doubling last year’s £17.2m. Its revenue grew by 7.1 per cent to £953m, helped by volume increases in categories like motoring accessories and tyres.

Halfords, which was founded in Leicester in 1892, is known for being Britain’s biggest bicycle retailer. But, after the Covid-era surge in demand for bikes faded, new boss Henry Birch has pushed the group to focus on expanding its garage business.

These efforts, which the company pitched to investors as its “Fit for the Future” strategy, were given a lift over the summer when it posted “very strong performance in seasonal categories, in part reflecting unusually warm summer weather”. 

Halfords overhauls retail ranges

Halfords said on Thursday that it expects this unexpected sales boost to “normalise somewhat” in the second half of the year. “Our focus on execution is nevertheless delivering sustainably improved returns,” the group added.

The company is now starting work on its “Evolve” agenda, which will see the group target between £10m and £15m in annual efficiency costs by simplifying its supply chain and operations.

Halfords has already started work on this programme by exercising closer control of the hours worked by its garage staff in a bid to cut labour costs, it said. “[By] ensuring we have the right technician doing the right job in the right location, we are reducing our cost to serve,” the group said.

The firm, which sells cycling and motoring accessories alongside its garage network, has started overhauling its product ranges in a bid to drive margins growth. Halfords hopes to achieve an operating profit margin of between five and six per cent in the coming years.

Birch said: “We continue to make strong progress as we deliver the ‘Optimise’ phase of our strategy, and our focus on improved execution also meant that we were well set up to capitalise on the warm summer weather.

“Looking ahead, we see clear opportunities to invest for long-term shareholder value creation. To this end, we are pleased to be announcing investment in a new, national distribution centre which will support the next phase of Halfords’ growth and drive attractive shareholder returns, ensuring we keep the nation moving for many years to come.”

The UK’s financial watchdog has admitted to “some errors” in the calculation of its multi-billion pound motor finance scheme just months ahead of a legal battle at the Upper Tribunal.  The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said on Thursday it had discovered an issue with its economic modelling and data classification that affected how it categorised [...]]]>

The UK’s financial watchdog has admitted to “some errors” in the calculation of its multi-billion pound motor finance scheme just months ahead of a legal battle at the Upper Tribunal. 

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said on Thursday it had discovered an issue with its economic modelling and data classification that affected how it categorised a “small group of loans”.

This mistaken data helped produce the 17 per cent APR reduction rule, which is used to calculate compensation by trimming 17 per cent off a borrower’s original interest rate to estimate and refund the extra interest they paid due to hidden commissions.

The regulator said the impact on average compensation would be less than £10, but it would affect headline provisions for lenders and ongoing litigation.

“We are sorry for the further uncertainty this creates for consumers and firms. We will provide an update on any further material developments,” the FCA said in a statement.

An average payout of £830 was pencilled in by the FCA as part of its final redress scheme, with qualifying agreements reaching 12.1m.

Overall costs for the industry were expected to come in at £9.1bn.

Threat of new delay for motor finance compensation

The FCA will face challenges from three lenders, Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes-Benz Financial Services, and Crédit Agricole Auto Finance, as well as the advocacy group Consumer Voice, at the Upper Tribunal in February.

City AM revealed in October court filings from the lenders had accused the watchdog of using complex economic modelling to justify its redress scheme.

The new legal battle follows the Supreme Court partially overturning a landmark ruling on car finance deals last year, rejecting claims that hidden commissions were automatically unlawful. But it found one customer’s undisclosed commission created an “unfair relationship”, leaving the door open for an industry-wide redress scheme by the FCA. 

The fresh complication to the redress scheme threatens to delay compensation payouts further. Two lenders were expected to serve expert evidence to the Tribunal as a pre-hearing measure on Friday. 

The FCA said it would discuss with the challengers and the court the “impact on this deadline” and “timeline for the ligitation”.

Some banks have opted to begin paying compensation early in a bid to move on from the saga. Barclays confirmed at the beginning of November it would offer motor finance payouts following the regulator laying the groundrules for those wishing to settle.

]]> 2483427Samuel Norman Samuel Norman Showcase Cinemas’ Imax deal proves the big screen has a big future https://www.cityam.com/showcase-cinemas-imax-deal-big-screen-future/ Thu, 26 Nov 2026 07:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2482147

When cinema visionary Mooky Greidinger makes a move, the industry pays attention. This is the man who took a small family-owned chain in Israel, merged it with Cineworld and helped build the world’s second-largest cinema group. So when the news hit last week that Greidinger is back in the UK, having acquired Showcase’s 16-strong UK [...]]]>

When cinema visionary Mooky Greidinger makes a move, the industry pays attention. This is the man who took a small family-owned chain in Israel, merged it with Cineworld and helped build the world’s second-largest cinema group.

So when the news hit last week that Greidinger is back in the UK, having acquired Showcase’s 16-strong UK circuit and signed a major deal with Imax to roll out laser systems at 12 of its sites, the sector took notice.

It’s a big, bold move. But it’s also highly significant for the message it sends out: cinemas are still big business, and they have a big future.

UK cinemas: From lockdown to new heights

Six years ago the sector was singing a very different tune. Lockdowns were devastating. UK attendance in 2020 was down 75 per cent on the previous year, leaving entertainment groups here and around the world needing huge government subsidies just to keep going.

But keep going they did, and as 2026 draws to a close, there are clear signs even beyond the Showcase deal that the sector is not just back but reaching new heights: innovating, transforming, developing new formats and ideas. It’s been a decade of challenge and change. And cinemas have listened.

Even so, in 2026, issues remain. Change is still happening. Struggling sites are closing down. Attendance and sales figures are still in flux.

Odeon and the blockbuster summer

A year ago Odeon reported a sharp drop in attendance but a big increase in box office revenue, thanks to higher ticket prices. We await Odeon’s full-year 2026 results, but we know that the summer was a golden one for the group. With a little help no doubt from Christopher Nolan blockbuster The Odyssey, Odeon’s summer attendance was 33 per cent up on 2025 – its highest figures since before Covid.

In fact the whole sector breathed a sigh of relief this blockbuster summer, thanks to The Odyssey and just behind that Spider-Man: Brand New Day. The net result: admissions in August 2026 passed 17m, an increase of 56 per cent on the same month in 2025. Since Covid, only the Barbenheimer phenomenon of July 2023 has drawn more people through the doors in a single month.

Showcase Cinemas and Imax: The lesson for Vue and its rivals

Just the news that UK group Vue needed to hear, if rumours of a stock market float are to be believed. But it takes more than a few big summer blockbusters for that kind of move. Vue has wisely invested big across its portfolio, with refurbs such as the transformation of its Finchley Road site in London, completed in September 2026.

If the Vue float rumour is the teaser for a future, rejuvenated cinema business, Mooky Greidinger’s Showcase and Imax deal is the all-star cast and the after-party combined. And it is a lesson: if cinemas are going to thrive in the modern era, they need the latest tech, and the best possible screens. And that means big bucks going in.

Take note. Because without major investment and smart portfolio management, all the blockbusters Hollywood can make won’t be enough. Leisure habits are changing. Cinemas need to offer more than just popcorn and a screen – Imax 4K laser screens are just one example – to get customers off their sofas.

That means expanding and diversifying your offer to customers. Transforming places and properties. Creating truly mixed-use leisure spaces, with enough excitement to entice the whole family.

The Light Banbury: Cinema as a leisure destination

Everywhere you look there are inspiring examples. To call The Light in Banbury a cinema would be like calling Oppenheimer a story about science. The multi-use venue, opened in 2022, is a complex of bars, food options, a climbing wall, mini golf, karaoke booths, darts, bowling, soft play, and yes, a cinema.

Opening when it did, after so much turmoil, might not have been possible had The Light been a cinema alone. But with so much to offer so many ages and group dynamics, it goes far beyond that. And it may just be the future of the mainstream cinema sector.

There are groups investing in their existing estates. There are groups expanding. Take the steady growth of Nottingham-based indie chain Savoy, mainly through acquisitions, taking the group’s portfolio to nine sites. Or the continued expansion of Everyman, notably in Elephant & Castle, where a future five-screen cinema will be one of the company’s biggest in London. And there are those inspiring local stories, such as the news that a new 10,000 square foot three-screen cinema is heading to the North Yorkshire city of Ripon.

Which cuts to the core of why cinemas matter, and mean so much to people and places.

The future of the cinema industry

It’s been a testing decade for cinemas. But there are signs like these everywhere now, not just of a renewal, but a renaissance in real-life experiences. Retail and leisure spaces aren’t just reviving. They’re being reborn, out of necessity. And we say now it’s cinema’s turn.

The message of the last 10 years wasn’t that cinema’s days are over. Far from it. The message was that people need more than just a movie to get them out of the house. So, the smart companies have given them more: games, sports, entertainment, food and film; rich, exciting places, unique to their towns and high streets.

These visionaries are creating places greater than the sum of their parts. They are writing the future of leisure and entertainment, and a tantalising sequel in the neverending story of the silver screen.

If my neighbour buys a winning ticket does our shared postcode entitle me to a share of the spoils? And what are her chances [...]]]>

Britain’s Olympic sports are battling rising costs while their National Lottery funding flatlines, warns Ed Warner.

Is my door in the draw? I’ve no idea. How does the Postcode Lottery work? If my neighbour buys a winning ticket does our shared postcode entitle me to a share of the spoils? And what are her chances of success? 

What it appears to this avid Planet Rock listener is that there are only two lotteries in the market. The Postcode one and another offering a chance to win hundreds of thousands of pounds if I text ROCK to 64100 and stand by to answer my phone on a Friday afternoon. National Lottery, where art thou?

The grand dame of British lotteries is in the news once again this week. The business pages report that the National Lottery’s operator Allwyn has postponed a dual listing for its shares. You can currently find them on the Athens Stock Exchange, down in value by a third since they first listed on 1 April this year by way of a merger with a Greek lottery company. 

Cue regurgitated stories of the controversial franchise war with incumbent operator Camelot that Allwyn won in 2022, and the company’s failure to meet revenue targets in its nearly three years of operating the Lottery so far.

This all matters for British sport because the nation’s Olympic and Paralympic programmes are heavily dependent on distributions from the “good causes” pot created by Lottery ticket sales, as are many grassroots sporting organisations. The same is true, of course, of a swathe of bodies across other sectors deemed integral to the nation’s identity and wellbeing, especially the arts.

Forget for now Allwyn’s bid boast that it would double the sums flowing to good causes – after all, bid promises in any industry must always be taken with a fistful of salt. Instead focus on the raw numbers. The latest data from the Gambling Commission shows an annual £1.6bn generated for good causes by the Lottery. However, the most recent three-month numbers reveal a 16 per cent year-on-year decline.

The current economic climate is clearly a challenge that any lottery operator would struggle to overcome. Inflation is eating into household incomes. 

It would be unrealistic to expect this squeeze to trigger a spike in sales of a product that offers a very long-odds possibility of winning a life-changing sum, or indeed of scratchcards that might bring a far smaller injection of cash. [Park at this point the debate about the morality of state-endorsed gambling products and their impact on some of the more economically vulnerable members of the population].

For recipients of National Lottery funding – and I write as one, being chair of GB Wheelchair Rugby – the impact of economic conditions is brutal. 

Our costs are inflating while the funding we receive from the Lottery via the state’s agencies, UK Sport and Sport England, flatlines. In real terms, this funding income is down by more than a fifth over the past six years. The same is true for most other governing bodies.

My fear is that the National Lottery is in irreversible decline, its competitors too numerous, its products out-dated and incapable of reinvention radical enough to reverse the venture’s tide, and any psychological link between ticket buying and benefit to good causes lost in the mists of time, never to be recovered.

Remember the football pools? A staple of my youth, watching my father tick off the score draws on his coupon during the 5pm announcement of Saturday’s results. They still exist, it appears, cunningly branded The Football Pools. The Telegraph recently cited experts believing that fewer than 200,000 people now play each month, a fraction of the peak of 14m in the mid 80s.

For the nation’s dreamers, from 19 November 1994 footy results on the radio made way for big-money balls on prime time Saturday evening BBC1, Noel Edmonds and all that. Not quite a “stop the nation” moment each week, but not far off. Seems an age ago now. The last live draw on the Beeb was 10 years ago next month.

The National Lottery may prove to have a long half-life, but its decay over time seems inevitable, to be eaten away by changes in behaviour of consumers lured by new and more agile competitors. 

The blurring of identities between lotteries and gambling can only be steepening the National Lottery’s decline. How to hold onto a share of a consumer’s mind (or wallet) when they are being bombarded by ads for sports betting and online gaming?

Meantime, lottery-funded British sports need to plot paths to greater financial independence. Politicians, too, would do well to reflect on the importance of sport to the nation and debate ways beyond the Lottery in which they can assist in securing its healthy future – both on the field of play and at the bank.

Rubber tickets

I’ve been positively surprised by the level of engagement – my own included – with rugby’s new Nations Championship format that has provided some coherence to the annual string of one-off contests in both hemispheres. I do, though, wonder whether a three-day, six-match finals weekend at a single venue is quite what teams and fans crave.

Better surely to have a pair of matches on a single day to rank the top four nations. Let the others have a weekend off. Do fans really care sufficiently about lesser rankings, or are these other games essentially dead rubbers? Ticket sales might give us the answer.

A sinister turn of events

A friend departing LGW in search of Moroccan winter sun bumped into an organiser of the World Association of Left Handed Golfers’ 30th World Championship, which is currently underway in Marrakech. 

Who knew? Good luck to all those involved. Are there any equivalent events in other sports, I wonder? Can’t find any on a quick Google search.

Ed Warner is chair of Sussex Cricket and GB Wheelchair Rugby and writes his sport column at sportinc.substack.com
