]]> Sequoia Capital’s decision to close its London office has reignited debate about the future of European innovation and the commitment of US investors to the continent – especially amid other departures including Andreessen Horowitz and Coatue. However, not all US investors in Europe share this gloomy outlook.

Thomas Bigagli, Partner and Managing Director at Plug and Play, believes the move says more about Sequoia’s investment strategy than Europe’s ability to produce successful startups.

On 4 November 2026, Silicon Valley-based Sequoia Capital announced it would close its London office, established in 2020, as part of a broader restructuring. The changes also include merging its early-stage and growth investment teams, simplifying its partnership structure, and discontinuing its Arc accelerator and Scouts programme.

The announcement follows similar decisions by Andreessen Horowitz, which closed its London office in 2025, and Coatue, which withdrew in 2024, raising questions about whether international investors are reconsidering their physical presence in Europe.

Speaking to EU-Startups, Thomas offered a different interpretation.

“I wouldn’t necessarily interpret Sequoia’s decision as a lack of confidence in European entrepreneurship, but rather as a reflection of an evolving investment strategy and operating model. […] That is fundamentally different from saying that Europe no longer presents attractive investment opportunities.”

Investing in Europe, or investing in its future?

According to Thomas, Sequoia is moving towards a leaner, more centralised organisation capable of investing internationally without maintaining offices in every market. For established startups seeking growth capital and access to US networks, this approach can be effective.

“However, it raises an interesting question about how international venture capital firms approach foreign markets: are you investing in an ecosystem, or are you genuinely invested in that ecosystem? There is a fundamental difference.”

For Plug and Play, a Silicon Valley-based investment and innovation platform founded in 2006 by Saeed Amidi, maintaining local relationships remains central to its strategy. The firm operates across more than 70 locations worldwide, including over 25 in Europe, and works with more than 600 corporate partners.

Its European journey began in Berlin in 2013, when it became the first investor in German fintech N26. Since then, its portfolio has expanded to include companies such as Owkin, Zama, Einride and FINN.

Thomas explained that local teams enable investors to identify founders before fundraising begins, establish connections with universities and understand the needs of corporations and institutions. These relationships can also translate into commercial opportunities for portfolio companies.

“Technology travels fast, but trust takes time.”

Plug and Play doubles down

This long-term approach appears to be paying off. According to a PitchBook ranking cited by Thomas, Plug and Play is the most active US investor in European venture capital by deal count.

“What I find particularly interesting about this ranking is that it is not the result of a recent strategic decision to invest in Europe. It reflects more than a decade of continuous investment in European ecosystems.”

In 2022, the firm accelerated its regional investment activity by establishing a dedicated European investment committee and strengthening local decision-making. Thomas says its European portfolio has more than doubled since then.

Looking ahead, Plug and Play plans to develop additional investment vehicles alongside European institutional investors, family offices and corporate limited partners. It is also strengthening its university partnerships and developing industry-focused AI Centres of Excellence to connect research, startups and established businesses.

“We believe that some of the most valuable investment opportunities and competitive advantages are built through years of developing relationships, earning trust, and actively contributing to local ecosystems, rather than simply accessing them when attractive investment opportunities emerge.”

Despite Sequoia’s departure, there are indications that American capital remains interested in European startups. According to PitchBook’s Q3 2026 European Venture Report, US investors participated in 22.2% of European venture rounds during the first nine months of 2026, the highest proportion recorded this decade.

Recent EU-Startips coverage from 2026 provides further evidence that US investors remain active in Europe. On 17 November 2026, less than two weeks after announcing the closure of its London office, Sequoia Capital co-led a €4.5 billion Series C round for British AI drug-discovery company Isomorphic Labs, alongside Greenoaks, with Andreessen Horowitz also participating. Earlier in the year, Sequoia led ElevenLabs’ €424 million Series D, while Andreessen Horowitz backed Stockholm-based Pit’s €13.6 million funding round.

Plug and Play, meanwhile, participated in Barcelona-based NeuralTrust’s €17.2 million Seed round, Lithuania’s Axiology (€5 million), France’s Orakl Oncology (€30 million), Swiss Aylight Zurich (€4.5 million), and French Davis AI (€4.6 million).

Thomas expects this participation to continue, although investors may become more selective.

“You cannot fully understand what is happening in Paris, London, Stockholm, Munich, Vienna, Warsaw, Lisbon, Milan or Barcelona simply by sitting in Silicon Valley. […] Ultimately, the importance of having a local presence depends on where and how you intend to create value as an investor.”

Europe’s next big test: Scaling up

Thomas sees particularly strong opportunities where AI intersects with Europe’s established industrial and scientific capabilities, including robotics, advanced manufacturing, biotechnology, energy, healthcare, space technology and cybersecurity.

“I believe Europe represents one of the most compelling and, in certain sectors, underestimated technology investment opportunities globally. [..] From an investment perspective, the best-performing European venture capital funds can generate returns comparable to their US counterparts.”

However, he acknowledges that the continent still faces substantial obstacles to building global technology companies, particularly fragmented markets, limited growth-stage financing, slower technology adoption and weaker exit opportunities compared with the US.

“Compared with the US, Europe suffers from market fragmentation, slower decision-making and technology adoption, limited access to growth capital, and insufficient institutional investment in venture capital. […] Europe does not have a talent or technology creation problem. It has a commercialisation, financing, scaling, and liquidity problem.”

For Thomas, addressing these structural weaknesses will require stronger European growth funds, greater institutional investment and more opportunities for successful companies to remain and scale within the continent.

“We need more success stories like Spotify, Revolut, and ElevenLabs. […] Europe should not aspire to become the next Silicon Valley. It should build its own model of technological leadership, inspired by its unique competitive advantages.”

Where does this leave Plug and Play and the like?

Ultimately, Sequoia’s restructuring illustrates how different investment philosophies are shaping international venture capital. While some investors are prioritising centralised operations, others see local presence as a competitive advantage.

“We want to be more than an American investor investing in Europe. We want to be a long-term partner in building Europe’s next generation of global technology leaders.”

And although Thomas would not be surprised if additional US firms followed Sequoia’s example, Plug and Play has no intention of joining them.

“We don’t see this as a reason to reconsider our European presence. Quite the opposite.”

]]> OPINION: AI will favour the companies built for AI, not adapted to it https://www.eu-startups.com/2026/11/opinion-ai-will-favour-the-companies-built-for-ai-not-adapted-to-it/ Mon, 23 Nov 2026 12:13:41 +0000 https://www.eu-startups.com/?p=376477 For decades, business leaders have been warned that the impending arrival of a new technology will completely reorder the corporate world. But for the best part of the last thirty years, it did not.  The web, mobile phones, cloud computing and social media, for example, were all predicted as disruptors that would sweep the incumbents […]

]]> For decades, business leaders have been warned that the impending arrival of a new technology will completely reorder the corporate world. But for the best part of the last thirty years, it did not. 

The web, mobile phones, cloud computing and social media, for example, were all predicted as disruptors that would sweep the incumbents aside.

With AI, however, the warning deserves more consideration. The reason is less to do with the technology itself, but rather who is best placed to use it, and that is increasingly becoming startups, rather than established companies. 

The web didn’t break incumbents

The common story of the web is that of upstarts bringing down giants, and the rankings seem to agree.

The world’s most valuable company in 1995 was a Japanese telephone operator. In the same year, Microsoft barely made number twenty on the list and Nvidia was just a startup.  Today Microsoft, Nvidia, Apple, Amazon and Alphabet lead the rankings, and just six of the largest companies in 1995 remain in the top thirty. 

Though on closer examination, the incumbents were not the disasters the ranking implies. 

Companies such as Exxon, Coca-Cola and Toyota, more than tripled their combined revenue between 1994 and 2024, meanwhile Microsoft grew more than fiftyfold. The web gave them access to better logistics, cheaper computing and wider reach.  Oil companies could use better software without becoming software companies. Carmakers could run a more efficient supply chain. And a wealthier world could buy more cars, soft drinks and pharmaceuticals. The incumbents benefited from the technologies that were supposed to be disrupting them. 

It is therefore unsurprising that business leaders often meet warnings about AI with scepticism.

Where AI goes further than the web

The businesses that didn’t survive the dawn of the web, such as film rentals and newspaper classifieds, were not simply slow to adapt, they were substituted. The web typically made companies more productive rather than redundant.  

AI shifts this balance. While early digitisation took information and transactions online, real people were still responsible for interpreting information, exercising judgement and making decisions. AI can now take on a substantial share of that work. This raises the question of substitution again, but this time for jobs that sit inside offices, rather than on high streets. 

The startup advantage

The existing structure of established companies is built around human specialisation. Different departments and systems to coordinate different skillsets. While this structure made scale possible, it now makes it difficult to rethink how work can be done, which is why simply introducing AI into existing roles can often fall flat.

Startups have the benefit of starting from scratch, they can design their business around AI from the outset. A small team can now do the work of hundreds, and the ones who remain can serve customers, handle expectations and set the direction of the business. 

In the web era, startups predominantly sold tools to incumbents. Today, startups can enter the same markets as established players, but with fewer layers and at a fraction of the cost. The difference is design, not effort. Hospitals, nurseries and restaurants will always need their existing structures, but if your employees are knowledge workers, AI can be the foundation for a far more efficient and cost effective company. 

What decides the contest

Incumbents have spent decades building their customer trust, brand, proprietary data and deep expertise. While these are incredibly valuable assets, they are merely a headstart, not a guarantee. 

The contest will now likely become one of speed. Startups have to earn trust and knowledge, and incumbents must rebuild how their organisation works. 

The second task may be more difficult. Startups can earn trust through transparency and delivering good work. For incumbents, the challenge is to dismantle a structure that employs and rewards the people they  have to depend on to change it. 

Build the company that replaces yours

Rather than looking for ways for AI to improve their current organisations, business leaders should instead ask how they would build them today, with no existing structure. 

Incumbents should not throw away what they have already built, but they can decide which parts add actual value. However, that is also to say the organisational architecture that implements those advantages are blocking a new way of working.

So the question now becomes; if you were starting from scratch today, how would you build a company designed to put yourself out of business?

Then find a way to build it first.

]]> Norse Atlantic is sounding the alarm over the state of its finances in a market update published this morning, 25 November.

“The Company’s financial situation is critical,” the airline said. “It is dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs and to continue its operations.”

The company added it was already in discussions regarding short-term financing, but warned that there was no guarantee that these discussions would be fruitful.

The airline has been loss making since its launch, and has been exploring a takeover or sale for some time already.

What’s gone wrong for Norse Atlantic?

Norse has struggled to make money since day one. Operating its own long haul flights did not prove profitable, so in recent years, the airline has been increasingly reliant on flying for other carriers.

At its peak, its ACMI deal with IndiGo accounted for six of its 12 Boeing 787 Dreamliners. Last year, revenue from its charters and ACMI contracts doubled, but even that wasn’t enough; Norse posted a $20.1 million operating loss.

The events of 2026 have not been kind to Norse. The airline was already losing money when the war in Iran sent jet fuel prices sky high. The airline had no fuel hedged at all, so was completely exposed to the increase. It reduced its flying, including its Los Angeles summer schedule.

In the six months to June 30, 2026, Norse recorded $292.3 million in revenue, a $40.4 million operating loss and a $94.6 million net loss.

Then, just as winter was arriving, the contract with Indigo unwound. One of its Dreamliners had come back in August after the Indian airline stopped flying to Manchester, and the agreement for the other five came to an end at the start of November.

Norse has agreed to fly for Pakistan International Airlines (PIA), but that contract only busies two of its aircraft. The airline still needs to make lease payments on its 787s, even if they’re not doing much flying.

Norwegian regulator piles more pressure on Norse

Despite its precarious financial position, Norse is being further pressed over issues in paying compensation to passengers.

The airline faces a penalty of NOK 8,000 (about $810) per day over unpaid passenger claims, Norway’s Civil Aviation Authority announced on 25 November. The regulator ruled against Norse in March regarding these claims, and had twice extended the deadline for a response from the airline.

Nina B. Vindvik, the regulator’s legal director, said Norse remained responsible for paying passengers despite its financial difficulties. The penalty has been accruing since November 20 and applies Monday through Saturday until Norse can show it has complied with the order.

]]> What is a hardened aircraft shelter, and why is the RAF using them at night? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/raf-aircraft-hangars-at-night-drone-threat/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:36:11 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57964 The Royal Air Force is reportedly putting aircraft under cover overnight as a precaution against drones. What that means for an aircraft depends partly on the building it is towed into.

The post What is a hardened aircraft shelter, and why is the RAF using them at night? appeared first on AGN.

]]> The UK’s Royal Air Force is moving aircraft undercover at night to protect them against possible drone threats, according to reports published by Sky News and The Times on 25 November.

The Ministry of Defence told ADS Advance it was strengthening security at military sites but did not confirm the reported aircraft movements.

Sky also reported that anti-drone netting was under consideration for aircraft that remain outside. Nets have been used by Russia to protect oil refineries from drone strikes, with mixed success.

In the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the vast majority of Russian aircraft losses have been on the ground. The US Air Force’s loss of a rare E-3 Sentry to Iran while parked offers further warning about the fragility of air assets when not in flight.

Why do RAF aircraft park outside?

Normally, most of the RAF fleet will be out in the open air. This is simply a question of practicality: Refuelling, light maintenance and general readiness are all improved by having an aircraft easily accessible.

The RAF owns some huge hangars, but these are not intended for mass parking of planes. The A400M Atlas maintenance hangar, opened in 2018, covers 24,000 square metres and is 28 metres tall. Despite its size, it’s only intended to house three Atlas aircraft at a time, to leave space for engineers to work around the plane.

The RAF’s large hangars are in high demand for maintenance, and aircraft requiring service will be prioritised for occupation. Added to this, these facilities are not designed to provide protection against attack.

Both the Times and Sky News said aircraft were being moved into ‘hangars and hardened shelters’ at night. A hardened shelter is quite different to a hangar, and an ideal place to store aircraft if a drone attack is suspected.

What is a hardened aircraft shelter?

A hardened shelter (HAS), or protective aircraft shelter, is a heavily reinforced hangar built to protect aircraft on the ground from attacks.

They are typically constructed from thick, reinforced concrete with heavy blast doors, and may be covered with plants or soil for camouflage. Each shelter will usually house either one or two fighter jets.

The idea of a hardened shelter is that it will provide protection against a range of potential threats:

  • Reduce blast damage. Reinforced walls, roofs and heavy doors help shield the aircraft from the pressure wave of a nearby explosion
  • Stop flying fragments. The shelter can intercept shrapnel and debris that could puncture the aircraft’s skin, canopy or fuel tanks
  • Conceal the aircraft. With the doors closed, an observer overhead cannot see which aircraft is inside or whether the shelter is occupied
  • Separate the aircraft: Housing jets in individual shelters puts a reinforced barrier between them, reducing the chance that one blast damages several aircraft.

The UK’s air force has a long history with hardened shelters. At the former RAF Upper Heyford in Oxfordshire, Cold War aircraft shelters were built with reinforced concrete and heavy sliding doors. Some now form part of a scheduled monument.

During the Cold War, hardened shelters proliferated in the UK and in other NATO nations. Although some of these are now decommissioned, the MOD has maintained a range of hardened facilities to protect and store its assets.

The RAF regularly moves fighter-sized aircraft to hardened shelters if they’re not going to be required immediately, as they give the jets protection against the elements. What remains unknown is whether a mass movement is occurring as a result of a threat; if so, it will be the larger aircraft that prove more challenging to find storage for.

What has the Ministry of Defence confirmed?

“We take the security of our bases, equipment and personnel very seriously and are always adapting to counter any potential threats,” an MoD spokesperson told ADS Advance.

The spokesperson said the ministry was investing an additional £470 million in military site security, including physical protection, surveillance and counter-drone capabilities. It has also introduced restricted airspace over 44 critical defence sites.

The reports appeared a day after the ministry and the National Protective Security Authority, part of MI5, warned UK companies supplying Ukraine’s armed forces of a growing Russian sabotage threat. That alert was addressed to businesses.

Officials have drawn no public link between it and the reported decision about where RAF aircraft spend the night.

]]> How spy planes collect intelligence without being detected https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/how-spy-planes-avoid-detection/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 17:07:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56924 From stealth drones to airborne radar aircraft, modern spy planes use very different methods to gather intelligence and survive in contested airspace.

The post How spy planes collect intelligence without being detected appeared first on AGN.

]]> When asking how spy planes manage to collect intelligence without being detected, the answer, most of the time, is that they don’t. But not being detected and not being intercepted are two very different things. Some ‘spy planes’ are designed to operate undetected; others are not.

The category of ‘spy plane’ or reconnaissance aircraft is extremely broad. It can include everything from the famous high-Mach SR-71 Blackbird to E-7 Wedgetail AWACS to extremely secretive RQ-180s to even the F-35 fighter jet.

Most spy planes are veritable beacons

In some cases, spy aircraft are the exact opposite of stealthy or difficult-to-detect aircraft. Aircraft like the E-3A Sentry, A-50U Mainstay, and the E-7 Wedgetail constantly beam powerful radio frequency (RF) energy across the sky to track aircraft, ships, and other targets or objects of interest.

To modern long-range enemy radars, these beams light up the aircraft like the proverbial Christmas tree, even without considering the aircraft’s massive radar cross-section (RCS). Modern AWACS also have passive detection capabilities, although their RCS remains.

Reconnaissance aircraft actively emit to detect enemy aircraft. They are not trying to hide: their job is to illuminate the battlespace and provide information to friendly forces.

AWACS aircraft are extremely detectable, almost by definition. This likely contributed to Ukraine shooting down two of Russia’s rare A-50Us and featured in wider debates surrounding the US Air Force announcing it would abandon efforts to purchase the E-7 Wedgetail.

The USAF has since reversed its position on the E-7, but the inherent vulnerability remains. For these aircraft to remain viable, they have to be operated deep behind the lines, out of range of enemy air defences and where they can be effectively protected.

During peacetime, these aircraft are extensively operated in allied and international airspace to monitor hotspots, such as Kaliningrad and the Black Sea. In a hot war, these flights would likely be more challenging and may require aircraft to operate further from contested airspace.

Flying higher and faster

In the early Cold War, the United States Air Force looked to altitude and speed to protect its spy aircraft. The famous Lockheed U-2 Dragon Lady was designed to fly at altitudes of around 70,000 feet, out of range of Soviet air defence.

But Soviet air defences quickly developed, and Gary Powers’ U-2 was shot down by the Soviets in 1960. The Air Force was already aware of the U-2’s vulnerability, and programmes that would later give rise to the SR-71 were already underway.

The SR-71 did have some RCS-reduction features, but it was not a stealth aircraft and was not intended to remain undetected by Soviet air defence.

Instead, it relied on speed (Mach 3+ in dashes) and altitude (80,000+ feet) to evade air defence. Famously, its pilots have claimed it outran numerous Soviet and other enemy interceptor missiles over its career and was never shot down.

Separately, 2026 has seen credible speculation that NASA is gearing up to use a formerly retired SR-71 airframe as a testbed for new high-Mach technologies, likely engines.

Together with an overall race to develop hypersonic systems, Skunk Works’ reported SR-72 development effort, and Hermeus’s stated ambitions, the future of spy aircraft may include a return to high-Mach.

Operating outside of enemy airspace

An important dimension often left out of the conversation about the controversial retirement of the SR-71 is that much of the work of spy aircraft moved outside of enemy airspace.

Violating a nation’s airspace is considered a hostile act and carries political consequences. In some circumstances, repeated or deliberate violations may be viewed as highly escalatory.

Since the SR-71 debuted, a range of systems have emerged to fill much of the role without violating airspace. These include satellites operating far beyond a nation’s airspace and longer-range information collection capabilities such as SIGINT.

This is not to say that the need to overfly enemy airspace is gone. In practice, countries like the US typically fly uncrewed systems like the MQ-9 Reaper and RQ-170 Sentinel over enemy and contested airspace.

Drones are seen as less escalatory, and their loss carries far less political risk. Some of these systems (e.g., MQ-9) have been routinely detected and shot down by Iranians and Houthis in recent years.

Modern combat aircraft as spy aircraft

Perhaps one of the most significant aspects of modern 5th- and upcoming 6th-generation combat is the extent to which they blur Cold War-era fighter, bomber, reconnaissance, attack, and other categories.

The F-35A, as a multirole fighter, doesn’t just mean it takes on fighter jet attack and air superiority roles, but it is increasingly moving into the reconnaissance domain as well. It is, at least in part, a spy plane by some definitions.

The F-35A is designed to be stealthy and use a range of passive and active sensors. It can be the quarterback, quietly sensing its environment and passing that information to other platforms (e.g., Typhoons, F-15s) to engage.

Ongoing Block 4 upgrades are set to significantly expand the F-35A’s capabilities in these domains. It is also receiving a new active AN/APG-85 AESA radar that can be used for missions from improved detection to increased jamming and electronic warfare.

Northrop Grumman’s incoming B-21 Raider is expected to take this concept further. It will be much more than a stealth bomber; the USAF expects it to be a stealthy scout and sensor in its own right, eventually flying with loyal wingman drones.

These aircraft operate in a complex network of systems, which makes them increasingly difficult to discuss in isolation.

B-21 Raider completes first weapons-release test as bomber enters new phase B-21 Raider completes first weapons-release test as bomber enters new phase

Actual stealth spy planes

Perhaps the best examples of a dedicated spy airplane are the secretive RQ-170 (confirmed to exist) and the RQ-180 (strongly believed to exist).

As these flying wing drones are secretive, it is difficult to say much about them. That said, it is clear they use many of the same stealth (low-observable) characteristics found on the B-2 Spirit bomber and subsequent stealth fighters.

As stated above, emitting is, generally speaking, a sure-fire way to be detected. These aircraft are likely to combine low-observable airframe designs with sophisticated electronic warfare systems, passive electro-optical sensors, and carefully managed radio-frequency emissions.

Stealth does not make an aircraft literally invisible, but it can significantly reduce the distances at which hostile systems can detect, identify, and track it.

Finally, spy or reconnaissance aircraft are generally some of the most secretive of all military aircraft programmes. If the USAF or other major air forces operate types of classified military aircraft undisclosed to the public, chances are high that they are in this broad category.

]]> Why NATO still relies on a Cold War-era Boeing 707 to monitor Russia https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/nato-e3a-awacs-fleet-availability/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:22:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57881 NATO's E-3 Sentry fleet appears to be operating at half strength, but the fleet needs to continue operating until replacements arrive in 2035.

The post Why NATO still relies on a Cold War-era Boeing 707 to monitor Russia appeared first on AGN.

]]> Following November’s violation of Polish airspace by three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles, NATO authorized the forward deployment of a Boeing E-3A AWACS aircraft to reinforce surveillance over Poland.

These are 1980s-era radar aircraft based on the old quad-engined Boeing 707 airliner. The last scheduled passenger Boeing 707 flight took place in the US in 1983, although they continued flying until 2013 in Iran. Today, NATO is struggling to keep these ageing aircraft flying until replacements arrive.

NATO’s E-3A Sentry Component

NATO states that its “E-3A Component has fourteen E-3A aircraft.” The operational fleet is considerably lower. NATO owns and operates these assets, with personnel drawn from multiple member countries.

Originally, NATO ordered a fleet of 18 aircraft in 1978. One crashed in 1996, another was cannibalized for spares in 2015, and two were retired in 2017 and 2018.

NATO describes its operational E-3 squadrons as having integrated international personnel from 19 different countries. There are approximately 22 multinational operational aircrews assigned to the two operational squadrons, in addition to the training organisation.

A single mission may have mixed crews drawn from different NATO countries.

The importance of E-3 Sentry aircraft to NATO

These aircraft are able to give the alliance eyes and ears over the airspace. The massive rotating dome uses a pulse Doppler radar that gives early warning of low- or high-flying aircraft operating over the territory of a potential aggressor.

They are able to detect, track, identify, and report potentially hostile aircraft operating at low altitudes, as well as to provide fighter control of Allied aircraft.

They can monitor airspace out to around 400 km, and three aircraft operating in overlapping, coordinated orbits can provide unbroken radar coverage of the whole of Central Europe.

NATO notes, “Information collected by AWACS can be transmitted directly – via digital links – from the aircraft to other users on land, at sea or in the air in near real time.”

Poland’s airborne early warning and control capabilities are currently based on two Saab 340s equipped with the Erieye system.

NATO’s ageing fleet of E-3 Sentries not at full strength

According to OSINT analyst Steffan Watkins, in an updated post, of NATO’s fleet of 14 E-3A Sentry aircraft, six, or 44%, have flown in the past 28 days and aren’t in a maintenance facility.

Three were located at NATO Air Base Geilenkirchen in Germany, and one at Germany’s Wunstorf Air Base. The other two were in Spain and Lithuania.

Much of the remainder of the fleet appears to exist more on paper than in reality. One of these aircraft (registered LX-N90452) hasn’t flown since the end of 2021, or around five years.

Another aircraft hasn’t flown since mid-2023, and two more apparently last flew in 2024; two more last flew in 2025. Of the last two, one has not flown for 139 days, while one flew less than a week ago, but seems to have entered maintenance.

It is difficult to say how many of these are in maintenance and will return to service and how many are effectively stored. Multinational crews from across the alliance operate them.

First Boeing E-7 Wedgetail arrives for RAF service in Scotland First Boeing E-7 Wedgetail arrives for RAF service in Scotland

From E-3 Sentries to Saab GlobalEyes

NATO received its first E-3 in 1982, with the last being received in 1985. The fleet is planned to remain in service until 2035. The aircraft’s airframe is old, but its systems have undergone several generations of upgrades. These aren’t just 1980s radar aircraft.

Replacing the aircraft is also extremely expensive, with countries incentivized to keep the existing fleet operating for as long as possible. The E-3s were to be replaced with a fleet of more capable Boeing E-7 Wedgetails based on the Boeing 737 airliner.

However, the USAF announced it would cancel its own Wedgetail order in 2025 and pulled out of the NATO effort to purchase the Wedgetail for the alliance.

This collapsed NATO’s planned acquisition, leading the remaining European NATO members to seek a European alternative.

At the July 2026 summit in Ankara, NATO said it will begin formal negotiations to acquire up to ten Saab GlobalEye airborne early warning and control aircraft.

While the last rotating dome is visually impressive, it is no longer needed. The E-3 was developed during the 1970s and 1980s, and electronic technology has advanced massively since then. Modern systems are far more compact.

]]> ESA’s Hera reaches asteroid struck by NASA in historic planetary defence test https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/esa-hera-reaches-dimorphos-dart-impact-damage/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 14:06:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57913 More than four years after NASA’s DART spacecraft struck Dimorphos, ESA’s Hera has arrived to inspect the damage and measure the asteroid’s mass.

The post ESA’s Hera reaches asteroid struck by NASA in historic planetary defence test appeared first on AGN.

]]> More than four years after NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft into an asteroid to change its course, the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has has arrived at the Didymos asteroid system to investigate the full extent of the damage caused by the collision.

ESA will unveil Hera’s first close-up images of the asteroid Dimorphos later today (25 November), following the spacecraft’s two-year journey through deep space.

The mission will establish how much the asteroid was physically altered by the impact, measure its mass and examine its internal structure. And the findings could help scientists determine how to deflect an asteroid should one ever be discovered on a collision course with Earth.

NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) demonstrated in September 2022 that a spacecraft could deliberately change the motion of a celestial body. Subsequent research revealed that the collision had also altered the asteroid’s shape and even changed its path around the Sun.

Neither Dimorphos nor its larger companion, Didymos, poses a threat to Earth.

Hera’s first images of Dimorphos will be presented at Berlin’s Museum für Naturkunde, with a live broadcast beginning at 19:45 CET (18:45 GMT).

ESA has chosen the museum’s dinosaur hall as the venue for the event. Some 66 million years ago, an asteroid impact caused a mass extinction that wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs.

“‘We’re here to put a dent in the Universe,’ is what Steve Jobs famously declared,” said Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli.

“Through many years of hard work our international collaboration managed to do just that, and for the very highest of intentions: to help make Earth safer.”

Carnelli said the event would also recognise the work of the mission team, which overcame initial difficulties securing funding, the COVID-19 pandemic and an approaching hurricane shortly before launch.

What happened when NASA crashed DART into an asteroid?

Launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in November 2021, DART was the first space mission specifically designed to test whether an asteroid could be deflected by deliberately striking it with a spacecraft.

The target was Dimorphos, a roughly 151-metre-wide asteroid orbiting the much larger, 730-metre-wide Didymos. The two objects form what astronomers call a binary asteroid system.

On 26 September 2022, the approximately half-tonne DART spacecraft struck Dimorphos at 6.1 kilometres per second, or nearly 22,000 kilometres per hour.

The collision was observed by the Italian Space Agency’s LICIACube satellite, the James Webb and Hubble space telescopes and ground-based observatories.

It sent millions of kilograms of rocky material into space, creating a trail of debris extending more than 10,000 kilometres. The debris remained visible for months.

Before the collision, Dimorphos took approximately 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit Didymos. The impact shortened that period by around 33 minutes, substantially exceeding NASA’s minimum expectations.

However, scientists subsequently discovered that the collision had done far more than change the asteroid’s orbit.

DART changed the shape of Dimorphos

A study led by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), published in March 2024, found that Dimorphos had undergone a significant change in shape.

Before the impact, the asteroid resembled a flattened ball and followed a circular orbit around Didymos. Computer models developed using spacecraft imagery, radar measurements and telescope observations indicated that it had become more elongated.

“When DART made impact, things got very interesting,” said Shantanu Naidu, a navigation engineer at JPL who led the study.

The researchers calculated that the orbital period had shortened by 33 minutes and 15 seconds, settling at 11 hours, 22 minutes and three seconds.

Dimorphos was also orbiting approximately 37 metres closer to Didymos than before the collision.

The findings supported the theory that Dimorphos is a rubble-pile asteroid, essentially a collection of rocks and dust held together by weak gravitational forces rather than a single solid mass.

Hera will now allow scientists to examine those changes directly and establish whether DART left a distinct impact crater or reshaped the entire asteroid.

How flying debris helped move an asteroid

In August 2025, NASA published further research based on images captured by LICIACube, which had separated from DART 15 days before the collision.

The small Italian spacecraft photographed the impact debris from several angles, capturing its closest image from just 85.3 kilometres above the asteroid’s surface.

Researchers estimated that the collision had dislodged around 16 million kilograms of dust and rock. Although this represented less than 0.5% of Dimorphos’s total mass, it was approximately 30,000 times the mass of DART itself.

The material thrown into space provided an additional push, making the deflection more effective than the spacecraft’s impact alone.

“The plume of material released from the asteroid was like a short burst from a rocket engine,” said Ramin Lolachi, a research scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center who led the study.

Dave Glenar, a planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, who participated in the research, said many near-Earth asteroids were expected to have a structure similar to Dimorphos.

“So, this extra push from the debris plume is critical to consider when building future spacecraft to deflect asteroids from Earth.”

Understanding how different types of asteroids respond to an impact will be important when designing future planetary defence missions.

NASA also changed an asteroid’s orbit around the Sun

Another discovery, announced by NASA in March 2026, revealed that DART had altered the path of the entire Didymos-Dimorphos system around the Sun.

Research published in the journal Science Advances found that the collision had changed the binary asteroid system’s 770-day solar orbital period by 0.15 seconds.

It was the first measurable alteration of a celestial body’s path around the Sun caused by a human-made object.

Researchers used radar measurements and observations from volunteer astronomers who recorded 22 occasions between October 2022 and March 2025 when the asteroid passed in front of distant stars.

“This is a tiny change to the orbit, but given enough time, even a tiny change can grow to a significant deflection,” said Thomas Statler, lead scientist for solar system small bodies at NASA Headquarters.

The discovery is particularly relevant to planetary defence. An asteroid detected sufficiently early could potentially be diverted away from Earth through a relatively small change in its velocity.

What will ESA’s Hera spacecraft investigate?

Hera, Europe’s first planetary defence mission, was launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida on 7 October 2024.

The spacecraft flew past Mars on 12 March 2025, using the planet’s gravity to adjust its trajectory while also photographing its smaller moon, Deimos.

A further manoeuvre in February 2026 placed Hera on course for Didymos. Braking manoeuvres in October reduced its speed relative to the asteroids ahead of its rendezvous.

At the time of arrival, the asteroid system was approximately 195 million kilometres from Earth.

Built by a European industrial consortium led by Germany’s OHB, Hera weighs approximately 1,081 kilograms when fully fuelled. Its solar panels span 11.5 metres when deployed.

Together with its two smaller companion spacecraft, Hera carries 11 scientific instruments and a radio science experiment.

One of the mission’s most important objectives is to establish the precise mass of Dimorphos. Without that information, scientists cannot accurately determine how efficiently DART transferred momentum to the asteroid.

Hera will also investigate the asteroid’s internal structure, surface composition and altered orbit.

“How did the impact change Dimorphos? What is the mass of the asteroid and which of its properties explain its response to DART impact?” said Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS and the Observatoire de la Cote d’Azur.

During the initial six-week survey, Hera will fly at distances of between 20 and 30 kilometres from the asteroids. Subsequent operations will bring the spacecraft within eight to 10 kilometres, allowing scientists to map their surfaces in greater detail.

Later phases will include 12 close flybys covering much of Dimorphos’s surface, including the DART impact site.

Two miniature spacecraft will investigate Dimorphos

Hera is also carrying two shoebox-sized satellites, Juventas and Milani, which are scheduled to be deployed in early 2027.

Juventas carries a low-frequency radar designed to examine the asteroid’s interior. The measurements could establish how rocks and other material are distributed beneath its surface.

Towards the end of its mission, Juventas will attempt to land on Dimorphos and use a miniature gravimeter to measure the asteroid’s extremely weak gravitational field.

Milani will examine the surface composition of both asteroids and study dust in their surroundings. It may also attempt a landing at the end of its mission.

The two CubeSats will communicate with Hera through inter-satellite radio links, allowing the main spacecraft to relay their scientific data to Earth.

The 25 Nov unveiling is only the start of Hera’s exploration, ESA’s Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers said ahead of Wednesday’s event.

“In the next few months we will be flying closer to the asteroids, and early in the new year will deploy a pair of shoebox-sized CubeSats to take extra risks and venture even nearer than the main spacecraft,” Kueppers said.

Could humanity prevent a future asteroid impact?

Although major asteroid impacts are rare, relatively small objects can cause considerable damage.

The 2013 Chelyabinsk event in Russia involved an asteroid measuring approximately 20 metres across. Its explosion in the atmosphere generated a shockwave that struck six cities.

ESA’s Near-Earth Object Coordination Centre in Italy works alongside NASA’s Center for Near-Earth Object Studies to identify potentially hazardous asteroids, calculate their trajectories and assess the risks they pose.

NASA is also developing its Near-Earth Object Surveyor space telescope to detect asteroids and comets that are difficult to identify using visible-light observations.

Early detection remains central to any attempt to divert a hazardous asteroid. The more time scientists have before a predicted collision, the smaller the change in its trajectory may need to be.

DART demonstrated that humans could deliberately alter an asteroid’s motion. Hera’s task over the coming months is to establish precisely how that happened and whether the results can be reproduced when Earth’s safety depends on it.

]]> Could Ukraine fly America’s retired F-15 Eagles? A former US general makes the case https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/us-retired-f15-eagles-ukraine-transfer/ Wed, 25 Nov 2026 13:35:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=57886 Why it arguably makes sense for Washington to transfer dozens of retired F-15 Eagles to Ukraine and why it is highly unlikely to.

The post Could Ukraine fly America’s retired F-15 Eagles? A former US general makes the case appeared first on AGN.

]]> Retired United States Air Force Lieutenant General David A. Deptula has written an opinion piece for Forbes arguing that the US should consider transferring 50-60 retired F-15C/Ds to Ukraine.

Deptula is now the dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies think tank. He is also a senior scholar at the U.S. Air Force Academy’s Institute for Future Conflict. The retired general recently returned from Ukraine, where he worked with the Ukrainian Air Force to improve its air operations.

The US has hundreds of mothballed retired F-15C/Ds

Deptula argues that Ukraine is in sore need of more fighter jets and that the US’s recently retired F-15C/Ds stored at the Davis-Monthan boneyard could be a solution. These have been replaced by F-35As and F-15EXs in US Air Force service.

He writes, “The United States should assess whether it can refurbish, equip, and transfer roughly 50–60 F-15C/D Eagles to Ukraine.”

The US has over 240 F-15C/Ds in storage at the Arizona boneyard, with more expected to join in the next few years. Some of these would require little work to be ready to be transferred.

Ukraine needs more aircraft in the air at any one point in time than it can manage with its existing fleet; fighter jets are indispensable for fighting off Russian air attacks.

Ukraine’s F-16s, Mirage 2000s, and legacy Soviet era fighters pay for these missions in heavy maintenance. He argues that with its fighters tied up in air defence, Ukraine lacks units to carry out offensive missions against Russia.

A case for sending F-15C/Ds to Ukraine

The F-15 Eagle is a much larger aircraft than the light/medium weight F-16 and can carry more rounds (940 vs 511 rounds) and many more rockets for short-range air defence. If older F-15s could take over air defence, then Ukraine’s F-16s could receive multirole missions for which they are better suited.

Some of the retired F-15C/Ds have received the APG-63(V)3 active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, giving pilots markedly better detection range, tracking, and reliability than the radars on the F-16s or any of Ukraine’s other fighters.

He says the strongest argument is speed, as it takes time to produce and deliver new F-16s, Gripens, and Rafales. It also takes over a year to train pilots and maintenance crews.

Deptula notes, “Introducing another fighter type will pose some challenges for Ukraine: pilot training, maintenance, spare parts, ground equipment, infrastructure, and weapons supply must be resolved before aircraft are transferred.”

Washington unlikely to transfer F-15C/Ds to Ukraine

Even under the Biden administration, Washington refused to transfer retired F-16 Fighting Falcons to Ukraine, even though it has hundreds sitting mothballed in its boneyard.

This is not to say Washington didn’t aid Ukraine with F-16s. It did and does. Washington provided critical training and other facilitation roles, but it insisted the airframes had to come from European stocks.

In the last few weeks of 2026, Ukraine is expected to receive ten ex-Belgium F-16s, two ex-French Mirage 2000-5F, and possibly two or so ex-Polish MiG-29s depending on that particular set of colourful negotiations. The first of 16 ex-Swedish Gripen C/Ds are to arrive in January 2027.

🇺🇦 Ukraine will begin receiving Swedish Gripen aircraft in January 2027, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on November 23 📸: Wikipedia 🔗https://t.co/QjBBLbvX8m https://t.co/5fT4TrDcLW

— The New Voice of Ukraine (@NewVoiceUkraine) November 24, 2026

There is some wisdom to the maxim “never say never”, but under the current Trump administration, it seems highly unlikely it would seriously consider transferring old Eagles to Ukraine.

The latest opinion piece is no revelation that Uncle Sam has deep stores of active and mothballed fighter jets that Europe collectively lacks. The latest piece is an opinion of what Washington could do if it chose to, not a realistic assessment of what it will likely choose to do.

Instead, Ukraine is looking long-term to Europeans for its fighter needs. Its ageing, worn-out, and attrited fleet of Soviet Su-25s, Su-24s, MiG-29s, and Su-27s is likely to retire at the earliest convenience post-war.

These will be replaced by a fleet of up to 250 fighters (subject to political, financial, and industrial constraints). The fleet is to be made up primarily of Saab Gripens (mostly new Es), Rafales, and older ex-European F-16s.

]]> Eight more Airbus A380s will require wing crack inspections before 31 January 2027. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) added the aircraft to an earlier list of superjumbos that need checks after Airbus found a potential problem with the wing mid-spars, structural members that help carry the wing’s loads. EASA says cracking in this part of the wing could weaken the structure if it goes undetected and uncorrected.

The new airworthiness directive took effect on 18 November. It replaces the emergency order EASA issued in June, when a check on one A380 turned up what the agency called “an unexpected level of findings”.

Further analysis brought the list from 16 aircraft to 24. Emirates operates 22 of the affected aircraft. Etihad Airways and Qantas operate one each, according to Aviation Week’s fleet data.

What the inspections are looking for

EASA’s December 2025 directive identified areas to check on both wings, including parts of the mid rear spar and the inner and outer mid front spars. A review of those inspection results led to the emergency order in June.

Aviation Week reported that hydrogen embrittlement had accelerated cracking in some wing spars on A380s that spent extended periods in storage. The process makes metal less able to deform under stress, so cracks can develop more readily.

When the 24 Airbus A380s need to be checked

The eight aircraft added in November have a January deadline. For the 16 already on the list, the original deadlines still apply. As AGN reported in June, five needed an inspection before their first flight after 24 June, with a limited allowance to fly without passengers to a maintenance site. The other 11 were permitted up to 25 take-offs and landings from that date.

Qantas told AGN in June that its affected A380, VH-OQI, was already in Dresden, Germany, for heavy maintenance. The airline said at the time that the emergency order would not affect its flight schedule.

Operators can count inspections they already carried out under the relevant Airbus instructions. The eight newly listed aircraft are subject to Airbus’s inspection instructions dated 6 November.

Aircraft coming out of storage need a check before flying

The November directive also changes what airlines must do when they bring an A380 back from long-term storage. An A380-841, A380-842 or A380-861 that has spent more than 12 months in storage needs a wing mid-spar inspection before it returns to service. The rule applies after each qualifying storage period.

Once an aircraft returns to service following a check under the directive, the operator has up to 36 months to inspect it again. The next check must also take place within 42 months of the start of the previous inspection. Whichever deadline comes first applies.

If inspectors find a problem, the airline must contact Airbus before the next flight and follow the manufacturer’s repair timetable. Airbus also asks for the results of checks that find nothing. Operators have 30 days to report, counted from the inspection date.

EASA says the November directive is an interim measure and further requirements may follow. The agency issued the directive ahead of consultation and asked for comments before 9 December.

]]> Boeing has secured a contract from the US Air Force (USAF) to build 15 additional KC-46A Pegasus tankers, just weeks after an independent study urged the service to reconsider further purchases of the aircraft in favour of a new generation of longer-range tankers.

The latest order brings the total number of KC-46As contracted by the US Air Force and international customers to 203.

The contract also comes at an important time for Boeing’s 767 programme. Commercial production of the widebody is scheduled to end in 2027, but military orders for the KC-46A, which is derived from the 767, will keep the production line running for years to come.

“We’re grateful for the trust the U.S. Air Force continues to place in our team,” said Jake Kwasnik, Boeing’s KC-46 programme vice president.

“The KC-46 plays an important role in enabling military operations around the world, and we look forward to building on that partnership while staying focused on delivering on our commitments to support the warfighter.”

Boeing has so far delivered 116 KC-46As to the US Air Force, six to the Japan Air Self-Defense Force and two to the Israeli Air Force.

The airframer said the US Air Force’s KC-46A fleet had accumulated more than 180,000 flight hours since the first aircraft was delivered in 2019.

US Air Force urged to reconsider KC-46 purchases

As reported previously by Aerospace Global News, a study by the Washington-based Hudson Institute questioned whether continued investment in the KC-46A would adequately meet the US military’s future aerial refuelling requirements.

The report, Resilient Reach: Redesigning Aerial Refueling for Contested Global Operations, was written by researchers Timothy A. Walton and Shane Dennin.

While acknowledging the Pegasus’s performance in current operations, the researchers argued that its range, fuel delivery capacity and survivability could limit its effectiveness in future conflicts, particularly across the Indo-Pacific.

“The medium-range KC-46A has performed well in contemporary operations and would play an important role in any conflict,” the researchers said.

However, their modelling suggested that a medium-sized blended-wing-body (BWB) tanker could refuel more than twice as many groups of combat aircraft as the KC-46A or support them at more than twice the distance.

Unlike conventional aircraft, a blended-wing design merges the fuselage and wings into a continuous lifting surface, reducing aerodynamic drag and potentially improving fuel efficiency. The further a tanker travels to reach other aircraft, the more fuel it consumes itself, leaving less available to transfer.

The study estimated that acquiring and operating 250 blended-wing-body tankers could save $15.5 billion over 30 years compared with an equivalent fleet of KC-46As. Those figures are based on computer modelling rather than the demonstrated performance of an operational tanker.

The US Air Force is already exploring the technology. In 2023, it awarded California-based JetZero a contract to develop a full-scale blended-wing-body demonstrator in partnership with Northrop Grumman.

The demonstrator is scheduled to fly by the end of 2027, although an operational tanker based on such a configuration remains some way off.

KC-46 Pegasus: A programme beset by challenges

The latest order adds to a tanker programme that has experienced procurement controversies, development delays, technical difficulties and substantial financial losses for Boeing.

The US Air Force selected Boeing’s 767-based tanker in 2011 following a lengthy competition involving a rival proposal based on the Airbus A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport (MRTT).

The original programme envisaged the acquisition of 179 aircraft to begin replacing the ageing KC-135 Stratotanker fleet, which entered service in 1957.

Adapting an established commercial aircraft was expected to reduce development risks. However, integrating the military systems proved more complicated than anticipated.

Among the most persistent problems has been the KC-46A’s Remote Vision System (RVS), which allows boom operators to conduct aerial refuelling using cameras and digital displays rather than looking directly through a window at the receiving aircraft.

Problems with image quality under certain lighting conditions prompted Boeing to undertake a redesign of the system. The aircraft has also experienced difficulties involving its refuelling boom.

The programme’s fixed-price development contract has left Boeing absorbing billions of dollars in additional costs.

Despite these setbacks, the US Air Force has progressively expanded its use of the Pegasus in training, overseas deployments and operational missions.

Military orders extend the life of the Boeing 767

The additional tanker order is also significant for the future of Boeing’s 767 manufacturing operations at Everett, Washington.

As previously reported by AGN, Boeing is expected to conclude production of the commercial 767-300F freighter in 2027 ahead of the introduction of tighter international aircraft emissions requirements.

The 767 first flew in 1981 and became a widely used twin-engine widebody on domestic and international passenger routes.

Boeing delivered its final passenger 767-300ER in 2014 as airlines increasingly turned to newer aircraft, including the 787 Dreamliner.

Demand from cargo operators subsequently helped sustain production, with FedEx and UPS among the principal customers for the factory-built 767 freighter.

However, Boeing has not developed a freighter version of the 787, leaving it without a direct replacement for the 767-300F in the same market segment.

Military production will continue beyond the commercial manufacturing deadline.

The KC-46A is derived from the 767-200ER, incorporating elements of the 767 freighter’s design, reinforced structures, military communications equipment and cockpit technology developed for the 787 Dreamliner.

The tanker can carry approximately 212,000lb (96,160kg) of fuel and is powered by two Pratt & Whitney PW4062 engines.

It can refuel aircraft using both flying-boom and probe-and-drogue systems, allowing it to support a wide range of US and allied military aircraft.

The Pegasus can also be configured to carry passengers, cargo and patients requiring aeromedical evacuation.

Growing operational role for the KC-46A

Boeing highlighted recent KC-46A missions supporting humanitarian assistance, including the transportation of relief supplies under the US government’s Denton Humanitarian Assistance Program.

The aircraft has also participated in bilateral training involving the US and Japanese air forces, while long-distance deployments from Travis Air Force Base in California to Japan have supported operations across the Pacific.

The US Air Force, meanwhile, faces the challenge of replacing hundreds of ageing KC-135s while determining what kind of tanker it will require in the coming decades.

 .et_pb_column { position: relative; } </style> <style id="sie-custom-header-inline">/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 SIE Custom Header — v1.1.2
 Zero-CLS, no JavaScript layout shifts.
 No panoramic image — lean 64px nav bar only.
 backdrop-filter is intentionally NOT used on .sie-hdr__bar.
 Any element with backdrop-filter becomes a CSS containing block for
 position:fixed descendants, which would trap the user-ui mobile bottom bar
 (position:fixed; bottom:0) inside the header instead of the viewport.
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 /* 2026-11-08: bar moved from bright brand blue (#0056b3) to the navy the
 homepage redesign uses (#12233D), so header, hero and institutions band
 share one anchor colour. To revert, put #0056b3 / 0.15 back. */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #12233D;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: flex !important;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.
 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}
/* ── Responsive ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 :root {
 --sie-hdr-bar-h: 56px;
 }
 .sie-hdr {
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: flex;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav {
 /* Hidden off-screen when closed — no layout shift */
 position: absolute;
 top: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);           /* flush below the nav bar */
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter — same reason as .sie-hdr__bar */
 padding: 12px 0 20px;
 clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);       /* collapses upward — no CLS */
 transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
 z-index: 9998;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {
 clip-path: inset(0);
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list a,
 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 position: static;
 box-shadow: none;
 border-radius: 0;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06);
 padding: 4px 0 4px 16px;
 margin: 4px 0;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.8);
 font-size: 14px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
 color: #fff;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 480px) {
 .sie-hdr__inner {
 padding: 0 16px;
 gap: 16px;
 }
}
/* Hover-gap fix: invisible bridge spanning the 6px gap between the nav item
 and the dropdown panel, so the cursor never "leaves" while crossing. */
.sie-hdr__dropdown::before {
 content: "";
 position: absolute;
 top: -10px;
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 height: 10px;
}
/* Anti-FOUC guard for body-rendered overlays: their own CSS arrives 20KB+
 later in the HTML stream, so on slow connections they paint fully visible
 (the destinations grid "opens" during load). Force the CLOSED state from
 first paint — each component's .open/.is-open rules override these. */
.sie-dest-panel,
#sie-auth-drawer,
#sie-lead-form-drawer,
.sie-finder-overlay {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
} </style> <style id="sie-etmodules-font-display">@font-face{font-family:"ETmodules";src:url("https://www.studyineurope.eu/core/views/86f0928314/css/base/modules.woff") format("woff");font-style:normal;font-weight:normal;font-display:swap;}</style><meta name='robots' content='index, follow, max-image-preview:large, max-snippet:-1, max-video-preview:-1' /> <style id="sie-hide-divi-header"> /* Hide Divi's header (Theme Builder + classic) */

 /* Leonardo's panel: the button and its verified line read as one block,
